title: The Pill with Nothing Inside
paragraphs: Imagine you have a headache, and a doctor hands you a small white [[capsule|L6-0116]]. Twenty minutes later, your [[discomfort|L6-0259]] begins to fade, so you [[infer|L6-0448]] that the medicine worked. But what if the capsule contained nothing but sugar? Surprisingly, many people in this situation still report feeling better. This is known as the placebo effect.

The word "placebo" [[originated|L6-0617]] in Latin, where it means "I shall please." In [[medieval|L6-0548]] Europe, it was the first word of a song sung for the dead, and people who were paid to [[mourn|L6-0576]] at funerals were sometimes called "placebos" because they were not really sad. By the late 1700s, doctors were using the word for a treatment given more to please a patient than to cure him.

Today, placebos play an important role in medical research. When scientists test a new drug, they often give one group the real medicine and another group a fake pill that looks exactly the same. Only if the real drug works clearly better than the fake one is it [[deemed|L6-0225]] effective. Researchers have also found that the effect can be [[enhanced|L6-0305]] in surprising ways. In some studies, two fake pills worked better than one, and the color of a pill changed how people felt about it.

How can an empty pill [[soothe|L6-0839]] real pain? Experts believe that simply expecting relief can lead the brain to release its own natural chemicals that reduce pain. The sight of a doctor's white coat or the taste of a warm [[beverage|L6-0083]] may [[evoke|L6-0316]] memories of being cared for, and the body responds. This is one reason a kind [[caretaker|L6-0123]] can make such a difference to a patient.

Still, the placebo effect has limits. It can change how much pain people feel or how tired they are, but it cannot heal a broken bone or kill harmful bacteria. So should we [[discard|L6-0254]] real medicine and take sugar pills instead? Of course not. But the placebo effect reminds us that the mind and the body are closely linked, and that hope itself can be part of healing.
zh: 想像你頭痛，醫生遞給你一顆白色的小膠囊。二十分鐘後，你的不適開始消退，於是你推論是藥發揮了作用。但如果那顆膠囊裡裝的只有糖呢？令人驚訝的是，處在這種情況下的許多人仍然表示感覺好多了。這就是所謂的「安慰劑效應」。
placebo 這個字源自拉丁文，意思是「我將使人喜悅」。在中世紀的歐洲，它是一首為亡者所唱的歌的第一個字；而受雇在喪禮上哀悼的人，有時就被稱為 placebo，因為他們的悲傷並不是真的。到了 18 世紀後期，醫生開始用這個字來指一種「主要是為了讓病人高興、而不是為了治好他」的治療。
如今，安慰劑在醫學研究中扮演重要的角色。科學家測試新藥時，常讓一組人服用真正的藥，另一組人服用外觀一模一樣的假藥丸。只有當真藥的效果明顯優於假藥時，它才會被認定為有效。研究人員也發現，這種效應能以令人意想不到的方式被增強。在一些研究中，吃兩顆假藥比吃一顆效果更好，而藥丸的顏色也會改變人們對它的感受。
一顆空的藥丸怎麼能緩和真實的疼痛呢？專家認為，光是期待疼痛獲得緩解，就可能讓大腦釋放出自身能減輕疼痛的天然化學物質。看到醫生的白袍，或嚐到一杯溫熱的飲料，可能會喚起被人照顧的回憶，而身體也會隨之反應。這也是為什麼一位親切的照顧者能對病人產生這麼大的影響。
不過，安慰劑效應仍有其限度。它能改變人們感受到的疼痛程度或疲倦的程度，卻無法治好骨折，也無法殺死有害的細菌。那麼，我們應該丟掉真正的藥，改吃糖丸嗎？當然不是。但安慰劑效應提醒我們，心理和身體緊密相連，而希望本身也可以是療癒的一部分。

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why were some paid mourners in medieval Europe called "placebos"?
options: They sang songs to please sick patients.
They gave fake medicine to the dead.
Their sadness at funerals was not real.
They were the first doctors in Europe.
questions.explain: 第二段說受雇在喪禮上哀悼的人被稱為 placebo，是因為他們的悲傷並不是真的，故選 (C)。(A) 文中的歌是為亡者而唱，不是唱給病人聽的。
questions.evidence: people who were paid to mourn at funerals were sometimes called "placebos" because they were not really sad

questions.stem: Which of the following was found in some studies of fake pills?
options: Small pills always worked better than large ones.
Two fake pills worked better than one.
Fake pills could kill harmful bacteria.
The color of a pill made no difference.
questions.explain: 第三段說在一些研究中，吃兩顆假藥比吃一顆效果更好，故選 (B)。(D) 與文中「藥丸顏色會改變感受」相反；(C) 最後一段明說安慰劑無法殺死細菌。
questions.evidence: In some studies, two fake pills worked better than one

questions.stem: The word "deemed" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 只有真藥效果明顯優於假藥時，它才會被 deemed effective，也就是被「認定為」有效，故選 (A)。(B) 被當作有效的商品販售並不是這句話的重點。
questions.evidence: Only if the real drug works clearly better than the fake one is it deemed effective.

questions.stem: Which statement would the writer most likely agree with?
options: Doctors should give patients sugar pills instead of real medicine.
The placebo effect proves that pain is only in the mind.
Medical research no longer needs fake pills.
What patients expect can affect how they feel, though it cannot cure everything.
questions.explain: 作者說期待緩解會讓大腦釋放減輕疼痛的物質，但安慰劑無法治好骨折或殺死細菌，可見作者認為「期待會影響感受，但不是萬能」，故選 (D)。(A) 作者明確反對丟掉真藥改吃糖丸。
questions.evidence: It can change how much pain people feel or how tired they are, but it cannot heal a broken bone or kill harmful bacteria.

vocab.stem: Wash your hands before you cook; good ______ helps stop the spread of germs.
vocab.explain: 煮飯前洗手、阻止細菌散播，指的是良好的「衛生」習慣，故選 hygiene。captivity（囚禁）、intersection（十字路口）、astronaut（太空人）都和洗手防菌無關。

vocab.stem: With only a paper map, Lena managed to ______ through the narrow streets of the old city and find her hotel.
vocab.explain: 只靠一張紙本地圖穿過舊城的窄巷並找到旅館，是在「辨認方向、找路前進」，navigate through 是常見用法，故選 navigate。mourn（哀悼）、compute（計算）、deem（認為）都不能接 through the streets。

title: Nearly Eleven Kilometers Down
paragraphs: Far below the surface of the western Pacific lies the deepest known place on Earth: the Challenger Deep, at the bottom of the Mariana Trench. It sits in the Northern [[Hemisphere|L6-0412]], and its floor is nearly eleven kilometers below the waves. If the world's tallest mountain were placed there, its top would still be about two kilometers under the water.

For a long time, this dark world was [[virgin|L6-0975]] territory. Then, on January 23, 1960, two men set out to visit it. Jacques Piccard, a Swiss engineer, and Don Walsh, an officer in the US Navy, climbed into a vessel called the Trieste. Their cabin was a steel ball only about two meters wide, hanging under a huge float filled with gasoline.

The trip down took nearly five hours. In the dark, the men had only their lights and instruments to help them [[orient|L6-0615]] themselves, and they worried about a [[collision|L6-0160]] with the steep walls of the trench. Deep in the trench, they were [[stunned|L6-0872]] by a loud crack that shook the cabin. One of the outer windows had broken under the pressure. Instead of turning back, they kept going. The dive was a test of [[endurance|L6-0304]] as well as courage, for the cabin was cold and small.

When they finally reached the bottom, the Trieste raised a thick cloud of mud. This [[disturbance|L6-0271]] made it hard to see anything, and the men stayed only about twenty minutes before they began to [[ascend|L6-0057]]. Still, they had proved that it could be reached.

No one returned to the Challenger Deep for more than fifty years. In 2012, the [[renowned|L6-0754]] filmmaker James Cameron [[navigated|L6-0586]] a small submarine to the bottom alone. Since then, a few more people have made the trip, and robots have found that tiny creatures [[populate|L6-0680]] even the deepest trenches, where the water is almost as cold as [[polar|L6-0677]] seas. The deep sea [[spans|L6-0843]] most of the living space on our planet, yet only a small part of it has been explored. Like [[astronauts|L6-0062]] in space, deep-sea explorers have only just begun.
zh: 在西太平洋海面下的深處，有一個地球上已知最深的地方：位於馬里亞納海溝底部的挑戰者深淵。它位在北半球，底部在海面下將近十一公里處。如果把世界最高的山放進去，山頂仍會在水面下大約兩公里的地方。
長久以來，這個黑暗的世界都是未曾有人到過的領域。後來，在 1960 年 1 月 23 日，兩個人出發前往那裡。瑞士工程師賈克・皮卡德和美國海軍軍官唐・沃爾什坐進一艘名叫「的里雅斯特號」的潛水器。他們的艙室是一顆直徑只有約兩公尺的鋼球，懸掛在一個裝滿汽油的巨大浮筒下方。
下潛花了將近五個小時。在一片漆黑中，兩人只能靠燈光和儀器來確認自己的方位，他們也擔心會和海溝陡峭的岩壁發生碰撞。到了海溝深處，一聲巨大的爆裂聲震動了艙室，讓他們大吃一驚：原來是一扇外側的窗戶被水壓壓裂了。他們沒有折返，而是繼續下潛。這次下潛既考驗勇氣，也考驗耐力，因為艙內又冷又狹小。
當他們終於抵達海底時，的里雅斯特號揚起了一大片濃濃的泥雲。這陣擾動讓他們幾乎什麼也看不見，兩人只停留了大約二十分鐘就開始上升。儘管如此，他們已經證明了那裡是可以抵達的。
之後五十多年都沒有人再回到挑戰者深淵。2012 年，知名電影導演詹姆斯・卡麥隆獨自駕駛一艘小型潛水艇抵達海底。從那以後，又有少數幾個人完成了這趟旅程，而機器人也發現，就連最深的海溝裡都住著微小的生物，那裡的海水幾乎和極地的海洋一樣冰冷。深海占了地球上大部分的生物生存空間，但只有一小部分被探索過。就像在太空中的太空人一樣，深海探險家也才剛剛起步。

questions.stem: What happened to the Trieste during its trip down?
options: It hit the walls of the trench.
One of its outer windows broke.
Its float ran out of gasoline.
questions.explain: 第三段說一聲巨響震動艙室，原來是一扇外側窗戶被水壓壓裂，故選 (B)。(A) 兩人只是「擔心」會撞上岩壁，文中並沒有說真的撞到。
questions.evidence: One of the outer windows had broken under the pressure.

questions.stem: Why did Piccard and Walsh stay at the bottom for only about twenty minutes?
options: A cloud of mud made it hard to see.
The cabin was filling with water.
They had already found a new kind of fish.
Their instruments told them to leave.
questions.explain: 第四段說潛水器到達海底時揚起濃濃的泥雲，這陣擾動讓他們幾乎看不見，所以只停留約二十分鐘，故選 (A)。(B) 文中沒有提到艙內進水。
questions.evidence: This disturbance made it hard to see anything

questions.stem: The word "virgin" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ______.
options: under the control of the navy
questions.explain: 前文說這個黑暗世界「長久以來」是 virgin territory，接著才說 1960 年有兩人「出發前往」，可知 virgin 指「未曾有人到過的」，故選 (C)。(A) 那裡雖然危險，但不是這個字的意思。
questions.evidence: For a long time, this dark world was virgin territory.

questions.stem: What does the writer suggest in the last paragraph?
options: Robots have now explored most of the deep sea.
Space travel is more important than ocean research.
Nobody wants to visit the Challenger Deep again.
There is still a great deal to learn about the deep ocean.
questions.explain: 最後一段說深海占了地球大部分的生存空間，卻只有一小部分被探索過，並說深海探險家的旅程才剛開始，可知還有很多未知等待發現，故選 (D)。(A) 與「只有一小部分被探索過」相反。
questions.evidence: yet only a small part of it has been explored

vocab.stem: The baby fell asleep as soon as her father began to sing a soft ______.
vocab.explain: 爸爸一唱就讓嬰兒睡著的輕柔歌曲是「搖籃曲」，故選 lullaby。glacier（冰河）、fragrance（香味）、collision（碰撞）都不能「唱」。

vocab.stem: This raincoat is made of ______ materials, not natural ones like cotton or wool.
vocab.explain: 和棉、羊毛這類天然材料相對的是「合成的」材料，故選 synthetic。renowned（著名的）、vigorous（有活力的）、polar（極地的）都無法和 natural 形成對比。

title: When a Beach Needs a Rest
paragraphs: With its white sand, clear green water, and tall cliffs, Maya Bay in southern Thailand looks like a picture from a dream. After it appeared in a popular Hollywood film in 2000, it became one of the most [[renowned|L6-0754]] spots along the country's [[coastline|L6-0159]]. Soon, thousands of visitors were arriving every day, many of them on noisy motorboats.

The crowds came at a price. Boats dropped their [[anchors|L6-0043]] onto the [[coral|L6-0192]] and broke it into pieces, while sunscreen and fuel polluted the water. Trash [[accumulated|L6-0013]] on the sand. By 2018, much of the coral in the bay had been damaged, and officials [[deemed|L6-0225]] the situation too serious to ignore.

In June 2018, Thai officials announced the [[closure|L6-0157]] of the bay. It was supposed to last a few months, but it lasted more than three years. During that time, workers [[transplanted|L6-0926]] young coral onto the damaged areas, and a type of small shark, which had largely disappeared from the bay, came back to swim in its shallow water.

When Maya Bay opened again in 2022, the rules had changed. Boats are no longer allowed to enter the bay; they stop at the other side of the island, and visitors walk in. Swimming is not permitted, the number of visitors at one time is limited, and each group may stay for only a short period. Travelers are expected to [[abide|L6-0002]] by these rules and to check them [[beforehand|L6-0082]].

Many people [[applauded|L6-0050]] the decision, though some local businesses worried about losing income. Maya Bay's story raises a question for every traveler: how can we enjoy a beautiful place without destroying it? Sustainable tourism tries to answer this by protecting nature and [[conserving|L6-0182]] resources while still welcoming visitors. Our own small choices can [[complement|L6-0169]] the rules: carry a [[waterproof|L6-0986]] bag for your trash, choose sunscreen that is safe for the sea, and stay on marked paths. The [[aesthetic|L6-0025]] value of a place like this is worth protecting, not only for us but also for those who come after us.
zh: 白色的沙灘、清澈的碧綠海水和高聳的懸崖，讓泰國南部的瑪雅灣看起來像夢中的畫面。在 2000 年出現在一部熱門的好萊塢電影之後，它成了泰國海岸線上最著名的景點之一。很快地，每天都有數以千計的遊客湧入，其中很多人是搭乘吵雜的汽艇前來。
人潮帶來了代價。船隻把錨拋在珊瑚上，把珊瑚砸成碎片，防曬乳和燃油也汙染了海水。垃圾在沙灘上越積越多。到了 2018 年，灣內有許多珊瑚已經受損，官方認為情況嚴重到不能再忽視。
2018 年 6 月，泰國官方宣布關閉瑪雅灣。原本預計只關幾個月，結果卻關了三年多。在這段期間，工作人員把幼小的珊瑚移植到受損的區域；一種原本幾乎從灣內消失的小型鯊魚，也回到了淺水區悠游。
瑪雅灣在 2022 年重新開放時，規定已經改變了。船隻不再被允許駛入灣內，而是停靠在島的另一側，遊客再步行進入。灣內禁止游泳，同一時間的遊客人數有限制，每一組遊客也只能停留一小段時間。遊客必須遵守這些規定，並事先查清楚。

許多人對這項決定表示讚許，不過也有一些當地業者擔心收入減少。瑪雅灣的故事向每位旅人提出一個問題：我們要如何享受一個美麗的地方，而不去破壞它？永續旅遊試圖回答這個問題：在持續歡迎遊客的同時，也保護自然、節約資源。我們自己的小小選擇也能和規定相輔相成：帶一個防水袋裝自己的垃圾、選擇對海洋安全的防曬乳，並且走在標示好的步道上。像這樣的地方所具有的美學價值，值得我們守護，不只是為了我們自己，也是為了後來的人。

questions.stem: According to the passage, how was the coral in Maya Bay damaged?
options: Visitors took it home as gifts.
Boats' anchors broke it, and the water was polluted.
Workers moved it to other islands.
questions.explain: 第二段說船隻把錨拋在珊瑚上把它砸碎，防曬乳和燃油又汙染了海水，故選 (B)。(C) 工作人員是把幼珊瑚「移植進」受損區域，而不是移走。
questions.evidence: Boats dropped their anchors onto the coral and broke it into pieces, while sunscreen and fuel polluted the water.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a rule at Maya Bay since it reopened?
options: Visitors must arrive by boat inside the bay.
Each group may stay as long as it likes.
questions.explain: 第四段列出重新開放後的規定，其中包括禁止游泳，故選 (C)。(A) 船隻已不能駛入灣內；(B) 每組只能停留一小段時間。
questions.evidence: Swimming is not permitted

questions.stem: The word "closure" in paragraph 3 refers to ______.
options: the act of shutting the bay to visitors
the end of the Hollywood film
a wall built around the coral
questions.explain: 下一句說它原本預計維持幾個月，結果持續了三年多，2022 年才「重新開放」，可知 closure 指「關閉瑪雅灣、不讓遊客進入」，故選 (A)。
questions.evidence: In June 2018, Thai officials announced the closure of the bay.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Hollywood films are the best way to promote tourism.
Maya Bay should stay closed forever.
Local businesses are against all rules for visitors.
Maya Bay shows why tourism must be balanced with protecting nature.
questions.explain: 文章敘述瑪雅灣因遊客過多而受損、關閉復育後再以新規定開放，最後談到永續旅遊與遊客能做的事，主旨是觀光需要與保護自然取得平衡，故選 (D)。(B) 瑪雅灣已重新開放，作者並未主張永久關閉。
questions.evidence: how can we enjoy a beautiful place without destroying it?

vocab.stem: Before the long flight, Mia packed her cookies in an ______ box so they would stay fresh and crisp.
vocab.explain: 要讓餅乾保持新鮮酥脆，應該裝在「密封的」盒子裡，故選 airtight（注意前面是 an）。aesthetic（美學的）、velvet（天鵝絨的）、coral（珊瑚色的）都無法讓餅乾保鮮。

vocab.stem: As the plane climbed to a higher ______, some passengers felt their ears begin to hurt.
vocab.explain: 飛機爬升到更高的「海拔／高度」時，乘客耳朵會因氣壓變化而疼痛，故選 altitude。banquet（宴會）、cavity（洞；蛀牙）、vanilla（香草）都不能用 higher 描述飛行高度。

title: Why the Bad Stays with Us
paragraphs: You give a presentation in class. Afterward, twenty classmates say it was great, but one says it was boring. That night, as you lie in bed, which comment makes you [[groan|L6-0394]]? For most people, it is the negative one. A single negative remark can [[haunt|L6-0406]] us for days, while the praise is quickly forgotten. Psychologists call this the negativity bias, and it is one of several biases, or habits of thinking, that can lead us to wrong conclusions.

Why do we [[dwell|L6-0290]] on bad news? One explanation goes back to early humans. For them, missing a sign of danger could mean death, while missing a pleasant surprise cost very little. A brain that paid extra attention to threats helped people survive. Today, however, the same habit can cause [[distress|L6-0270]] for no good reason. A tiny [[flaw|L6-0351]] in our appearance or one low test score can seem far more important than it really is.

Another bias affects how we judge risk. News reports of a plane crash [[evoke|L6-0316]] strong fear, and afterward many people feel that flying is more dangerous than driving. In fact, mile for mile, traveling by car is much riskier. Because shocking events are easy to remember, we [[infer|L6-0448]] that they happen more often than they do. The news itself may be [[credible|L6-0207]], but the picture it leaves in our minds is not complete. Some people even make [[drastic|L6-0281]] changes, such as canceling a trip, because of one frightening story.

The good news is that knowing about these biases can help. When a bad comment keeps playing in your head, remember that its [[duration|L6-0287]] is usually shorter than you fear. Instead of letting one mistake send your mood into a [[downward|L6-0278]] [[spiral|L6-0846]], write down three things that went well. In many cultures, it is [[customary|L6-0218]] to brush off praise politely, but it is worth letting kind words in, too. Confidence and friendships [[flourish|L6-0352]] when we notice the good as clearly as the bad.
zh: 你在課堂上做了一場報告。結束後，二十位同學說你講得很棒，但有一位說很無聊。那天晚上你躺在床上時，是哪一句話讓你懊惱得直嘆氣？對大多數人來說，是那句負面的評語。一句負面的話可能在腦中縈繞好幾天，讚美卻很快就被忘記。心理學家稱之為「負面偏誤」，它是幾種偏誤（也就是思考習慣）之一，可能讓我們得出錯誤的結論。
我們為什麼老是想著壞消息呢？其中一種解釋要追溯到早期人類。對他們來說，錯過一個危險的訊號可能意味著死亡，錯過一個愉快的驚喜卻幾乎沒有損失。一個特別留意威脅的大腦，能幫助人類生存下來。然而在今天，同樣的習慣可能讓我們無緣無故地苦惱。外表上一個小小的瑕疵、一次考不好的成績，都可能顯得比實際上重要得多。
另一種偏誤會影響我們判斷風險的方式。墜機的新聞報導會喚起強烈的恐懼，之後許多人便覺得搭飛機比開車危險。事實上，以每英里來計算，搭車旅行的風險高得多。因為令人震驚的事件容易被記住，我們便推論這類事件發生的頻率比實際更高。新聞本身也許可信，但它在我們心中留下的畫面並不完整。有些人甚至因為一則嚇人的報導，就做出取消旅行這類劇烈的改變。
好消息是，了解這些偏誤能幫助我們。當一句負面評語在腦中不斷重播時，要記得它影響的時間通常比你擔心的短。與其讓一個錯誤使心情陷入向下的惡性循環，不如寫下三件順利的事。在許多文化中，客氣地推辭讚美是一種慣例，但讓善意的話語真正進到心裡也是值得的。當我們能像看見壞事一樣清楚地看見好事時，自信和友誼都會茁壯成長。

glosses.zh: 負面性（negativity bias 負面偏誤）

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why might early humans have developed the habit of paying attention to bad things?
options: Noticing danger helped them stay alive.
They had no news reports to read.
Bad news was easier to share with others.
questions.explain: 第二段說對早期人類而言，錯過危險訊號可能致命，所以特別留意威脅的大腦能幫助人類生存，故選 (A)。(B) 文中說錯過驚喜「損失很小」，並沒有說驚喜很少。
questions.evidence: A brain that paid extra attention to threats helped people survive.

questions.stem: What does the passage say about flying and driving?
options: Flying is riskier than most people think.
Driving is more dangerous than flying, mile for mile.
News reports about car accidents cause the most fear.
People who fly often worry less about risk.
questions.explain: 第三段說許多人覺得飛行比開車危險，但事實上以每英里計算，搭車的風險高得多，故選 (B)。(A) 與文意相反。
questions.evidence: In fact, mile for mile, traveling by car is much riskier.

questions.stem: The phrase "a downward spiral" in paragraph 4 most likely describes ______.
options: a way of writing down good memories
a polite way to refuse praise
a situation that keeps getting worse
a short period of bad weather
questions.explain: 文中說不要讓「一個錯誤」把心情送進 a downward spiral，並建議改寫下順利的事，可知它指心情越來越糟、不斷往下的惡性循環，故選 (C)。(A) 寫下好事是作者提出的對策，而不是這個詞的意思。
questions.evidence: Instead of letting one mistake send your mood into a downward spiral, write down three things that went well.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How to give a good presentation in class
Why news reports should not cover plane crashes
How early humans protected themselves from danger
Why our minds focus on the negative, and how we can respond
questions.explain: 文章說明負面偏誤與判斷風險時的偏誤從何而來、造成什麼影響，最後一段提出因應方法，故選 (D)。(C) 早期人類只是第二段用來解釋原因的例子。
questions.evidence: The good news is that knowing about these biases can help.

vocab.stem: Be careful when picking mushrooms in the woods: some are ______, but others are poisonous.
vocab.explain: 和「有毒的」形成對比的是「可食用的」，故選 edible。dental（牙齒的）、hospitable（好客的）、credible（可信的）都不能和 poisonous 對比來形容菇類。

vocab.stem: Farmers add ______ to the soil to help their crops grow faster and stronger.
vocab.explain: 農夫加進土壤、幫助作物長得更快更壯的是「肥料」，故選 fertilizer。firecrackers（鞭炮）、fins（鰭）、distraction（使人分心的事物）都不能讓作物生長。

title: Slowly, or Not at All
paragraphs: The bus left Yun at the bottom of the hill, and the mist that [[lingered|L6-0510]] over the slopes swallowed it at once. Her grandmother's tea [[plantation|L6-0673]] lay far [[inland|L6-0453]], hours from the city where Yun had grown up. She had come only because her parents were working abroad for the summer, and she had already decided to hate it.

Grandma Lin was small, quiet, and [[obstinate|L6-0603]]. She refused to buy a machine for picking leaves, and she refused to let Yun help until the girl had watched for three whole days. "Tea is like a child," she said. "You [[nurture|L6-0597]] it slowly, or not at all." That was her [[motto|L6-0574]], and she repeated it so often that Yun began to say the words silently along with her.

At first, Yun's fingers [[itched|L6-0476]] for her phone, but there was no signal on the hill. With nothing else to do, she [[roamed|L6-0774]] the paths and began to notice things. Every morning, a small brown bird [[perched|L6-0656]] on the fence and sang the same three notes, and its song [[soothed|L6-0839]] her more than she expected. The bells on the gate [[jingled|L6-0481]] whenever the wind changed. One afternoon, Grandma handed her an old glass that [[magnified|L6-0535]] a single leaf until its tiny lines looked like rivers on a map.

Picking was harder than it looked. Yun's back hurt, and her first basket was turned away because she had torn the leaves. It was a [[hurdle|L6-0428]], but she was too proud to quit. By the end of July, her baskets were accepted without a word, which, from Grandma Lin, was the highest praise.

On her last evening, Yun climbed to the top of the slope. The [[fragrance|L6-0363]] of fresh leaves filled the air. Below her, the rows of tea curved around the hill, and beyond them the [[majestic|L6-0538]] mountains turned purple in the setting sun. It seemed almost [[miraculous|L6-0558]] that a place could change so little, and a person so much, in a single summer. When the bus came the next morning, Yun found herself whispering the words: slowly, or not at all.
zh: 公車把小芸放在山腳下，繚繞在山坡上的霧氣立刻就把車子吞沒了。外婆的茶園位在遙遠的內陸，離小芸長大的城市有好幾個小時的車程。她會來，只是因為爸媽這個夏天要到國外工作；而她早已打定主意，自己一定會討厭這裡。
林外婆個子小、話不多，脾氣卻很固執。她不肯買採茶的機器，也不讓小芸幫忙，直到這個女孩在旁邊整整看了三天才肯。「茶就像孩子，」她說，「你要慢慢養，不然就別養。」這是她的座右銘，她說了太多次，小芸都開始跟著在心裡默念了。
一開始，小芸的手指癢得想拿手機，但山上沒有訊號。既然沒別的事可做，她便在小路上四處閒逛，也開始留意身邊的事物。每天早上，一隻棕色的小鳥會停在籬笆上，唱著同樣的三個音，那歌聲比她預期的更能撫慰她。每當風向一變，門上的鈴鐺就叮噹作響。有一天下午，外婆遞給她一個舊的放大鏡，把一片葉子放大到葉上細細的紋路就像地圖上的河流。
採茶比看起來難多了。小芸腰痠背痛，她的第一籃茶葉因為把葉子扯破而被退了回來。這是一道關卡，但她自尊心太強，不肯放棄。到了七月底，她的茶籃已經能一句話都不說地被收下——而對林外婆來說，這就是最高的讚美。
最後一個傍晚，小芸爬上山坡頂端。新鮮茶葉的香氣瀰漫在空氣中。在她腳下，一排排茶樹沿著山丘彎曲延伸，遠處雄偉的山脈在夕陽下染成紫色。一個地方在一個夏天裡改變得那麼少，一個人卻改變得那麼多，這幾乎像是奇蹟。隔天早上公車來的時候，小芸發現自己正輕聲念著那句話：慢慢來，不然就別做。

questions.stem: Why did Yun go to her grandmother's tea plantation?
options: She wanted to learn how to pick tea.
Her parents were working abroad for the summer.
She had no signal on her phone in the city.
Her grandmother needed help buying a machine.
questions.explain: 第一段說小芸會來只是因為爸媽這個夏天要到國外工作，故選 (B)。(A) 她一開始打定主意會討厭這裡，並不是自己想學採茶。
questions.evidence: She had come only because her parents were working abroad for the summer

questions.stem: What happened to Yun's first basket of tea leaves?
options: It was turned away because the leaves were torn.
It was praised by Grandma Lin.
It was carried away by the wind.
It was eaten by a small brown bird.
questions.explain: 第四段說她的第一籃茶葉因為葉子被扯破而被退回，故選 (A)。(B) 外婆「一句話都不說地收下」是七月底的事，而且那是後來的籃子。
questions.evidence: her first basket was turned away because she had torn the leaves

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, "which, from Grandma Lin, was the highest praise" suggests that Grandma Lin ______.
options: often praised Yun in front of others
did not care about the quality of the tea
wanted Yun to leave the plantation
questions.explain: 外婆只是「一句話都不說」地收下茶籃，作者卻說這對她而言就是最高的讚美，可見她很少用言語表達肯定，故選 (C)。(A) 與她話不多、不輕易稱讚的個性相反。
questions.evidence: her baskets were accepted without a word, which, from Grandma Lin, was the highest praise

questions.stem: What can we infer about Yun at the end of the story?
options: She still hates the plantation and wants to forget it.
She has decided to stay with her grandmother forever.
She is angry that the bus came so early.
She has come to understand and value her grandmother's way of life.
questions.explain: 小芸原本決定要討厭這裡，最後卻覺得自己在一個夏天裡改變很多，離開時還輕聲念著外婆的座右銘，可見她已理解並珍惜外婆的生活態度，故選 (D)。(B) 她隔天就搭公車離開了。
questions.evidence: Yun found herself whispering the words: slowly, or not at all.

vocab.stem: Some people are shy at parties, but my sister is very ______; she makes new friends wherever she goes.
vocab.explain: 和害羞相反、走到哪裡都能交到新朋友，表示她個性「外向」，故選 outgoing。permissible（可允許的）、preventive（預防的）、inland（內陸的）都不能形容人的個性。

vocab.stem: Farmers in this valley raise ______ such as cows, sheep, and pigs.
vocab.explain: 牛、羊、豬都是農家飼養的「家畜」，故選 livestock。latitude（緯度）、parliament（議會）、orphanage（孤兒院）都不能用 cows, sheep, and pigs 來舉例。

title: Roads of Silk and Ideas
paragraphs: The name "Silk Road" [[evokes|L6-0316]] images of camels crossing deserts with loads of shining cloth. Yet the name was created only in 1877, by a German scholar, Ferdinand von Richthofen, long after the trade it describes had ended. And it was never a single road. It was a network of routes that [[spanned|L6-0843]] thousands of kilometers, linking China with Central Asia, India, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean.

The trade [[originated|L6-0617]] more than two thousand years ago, when China's Han Dynasty began to trade with distant peoples to the west. Chinese silk was the most [[renowned|L6-0754]] product, but merchants also carried tea, paper, and spices, while horses, glass, and silver moved east. Few traders traveled the whole way. Instead, goods passed from hand to hand, and their prices rose at every stop. The journey was full of [[hurdles|L6-0428]]: high mountains, burning deserts, and thieves. Only travelers with great [[endurance|L6-0304]] could survive it.

Along the way, many cities [[flourished|L6-0352]]. Samarkand, in Central Asia, grew rich as a meeting point for traders. Travelers could [[lodge|L6-0519]] at inns along the way and feed their [[livestock|L6-0516]], such as camels and horses. At these stops, it was [[customary|L6-0218]] for merchants to share meals and news, and local hosts were often [[hospitable|L6-0421]], since their own wealth depended on trade. Some travelers [[lingered|L6-0510]] for weeks, waiting for better weather or a new group to travel with.

However, the Silk Road carried more than goods; ideas and skills moved along it, too. Buddhism traveled from India into China, and the Chinese method of making paper slowly spread west, finally reaching [[medieval|L6-0548]] Europe. Such exchanges [[enriched|L6-0307]] cultures at both ends of the routes. Disease traveled, too. Many historians believe that the plague of the 1340s spread along these trade routes, and the [[outbreak|L6-0622]] caused a huge loss of life across Asia and Europe.

From the 1400s on, the land routes slowly became less important, partly because ships could now [[navigate|L6-0586]] the seas between Asia and Europe more cheaply. Yet the Silk Road has not been forgotten. In 2014, part of the network was named a World Heritage Site, and its ancient cities still attract visitors. Above all, it reminds us that connections between distant peoples are nothing new.
zh: 「絲路」這個名稱，讓人聯想到駱駝載著閃閃發亮的布匹、穿越沙漠的畫面。然而，這個名稱其實直到 1877 年才由德國學者李希霍芬創造出來，那時它所指的貿易早已結束很久。而且，絲路從來就不是單獨一條路，而是一張綿延數千公里的路線網絡，把中國和中亞、印度、中東以及地中海地區連結在一起。
這項貿易起源於兩千多年前，當時中國的漢朝開始和西方遙遠地區的人民進行貿易。中國絲綢是最有名的商品，但商人也運送茶葉、紙張和香料；而馬匹、玻璃和白銀則往東方流動。很少有商人走完全程，貨物通常是一手轉過一手，每經過一站，價格就上漲一次。這段旅程充滿重重障礙：高山、酷熱的沙漠，還有盜賊。只有耐力極佳的旅人才能走完全程。
沿途有許多城市因此繁榮起來。位於中亞的撒馬爾罕就是因為成為商人聚集的交會點而致富。旅人可以在沿途的旅店投宿，並餵養他們的牲畜，例如駱駝和馬。在這些停靠站，商人習慣一起用餐、交換消息；而當地的主人通常也很好客，因為他們自己的財富就仰賴貿易。有些旅人會停留好幾個星期，等待天氣轉好，或等新的隊伍一起上路。
不過，絲路運送的不只是貨物，思想和技術也沿著它傳播。佛教從印度傳入中國，而中國的造紙方法則慢慢向西傳播，最後傳到了中世紀的歐洲。這樣的交流使這些路線兩端的文化都更加豐富。疾病也隨之傳播。許多歷史學家認為，1340 年代的瘟疫就是沿著這些貿易路線散播的，這場疫情的爆發在亞洲和歐洲造成了大量人命損失。
從 1400 年代起，陸上路線的重要性逐漸降低，部分原因是船隻已經能以更低的成本，在亞洲和歐洲之間的海域航行。然而，絲路並沒有被遺忘。2014 年，這個路線網絡的一部分被列為世界遺產，它沿途的古老城市至今仍吸引著遊客。最重要的是，它提醒我們：遙遠民族之間的連結，並不是什麼新鮮事。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why silk was the most valuable product in ancient China
How the Silk Road connected distant peoples through goods, ideas, and even disease
How ships replaced camels in modern trade
The life of the German scholar who named the Silk Road
questions.explain: 文章介紹絲路名稱的由來、貿易的起源與困難、沿途城市的繁榮，以及思想與疾病的傳播，最後說它提醒我們遠方民族間早有連結，故選 (B)。(D) 李希霍芬只在第一段提到。
questions.evidence: It was a network of routes that spanned thousands of kilometers, linking China with Central Asia, India, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did prices rise along the Silk Road?
options: Goods passed through many traders' hands, and prices went up at every stop.
The Han Dynasty charged high taxes on silk.
Most traders traveled the whole way alone.
Ships could travel between Asia and Europe more cheaply.
questions.explain: 第二段說很少有商人走完全程，貨物一手轉過一手，每經過一站價格就上漲，故選 (A)。(C) 與「很少有商人走完全程」相反；(D) 是後來陸路衰落的原因。
questions.evidence: Instead, goods passed from hand to hand, and their prices rose at every stop.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the hosts at roadside stops?
options: They did not trust merchants from other lands.
They wanted travelers to leave as soon as possible.
They had good reasons to treat traders well.
They only welcomed traders from China.
questions.explain: 第三段說當地主人通常很好客，因為他們自己的財富就仰賴貿易，可推知他們善待商人是有實際理由的，故選 (C)。(B) 文中還提到有些旅人會停留好幾週，看不出主人希望他們快走。
questions.evidence: local hosts were often hospitable, since their own wealth depended on trade

questions.stem: The word "lingered" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 旅人 lingered for weeks，是為了等天氣轉好或等新隊伍一起上路，可知是在原地「多停留」，故選 (B)。(C) 快速趕路與「等待」的意思相反。
questions.evidence: Some travelers lingered for weeks, waiting for better weather or a new group to travel with.

vocab.stem: Please knock before you come in; I don't want anyone to ______ on my private time.
vocab.explain: 進門前先敲門，是不希望有人「闖入、打擾」自己的私人時間，intrude on 是固定用法，故選 intrude。magnify（放大）、nurture（養育）、perch（棲息）都無法表達「打擾」的意思。

vocab.stem: Washing your hands often is a simple ______ step against colds and the flu.
vocab.explain: 勤洗手是對抗感冒和流感的簡單「預防」措施，故選 preventive。majestic（雄偉的）、obstinate（頑固的）、miraculous（奇蹟般的）都不能形容洗手這個步驟。

title: Who Made This Picture?
paragraphs: In 2022, an image of a grand, glowing hall won first prize in the digital art section of a contest in Colorado. The picture was full of [[splendor|L6-0847]], but no one had painted it by hand. Its creator had typed descriptions into an AI program and chosen the best of the results. When the news spread, some artists [[rejoiced|L6-0746]] at the new possibilities, while many others were angry. The debate that followed [[revolves|L6-0770]] around one question: who is the real artist?

AI programs learn by studying huge numbers of existing images, many of them made by living artists who were never asked for permission. The programs can then [[reproduce|L6-0755]] an artist's style in seconds. For a painter who has spent years building [[proficiency|L6-0700]] with a brush, this can cause real [[distress|L6-0270]]. Some also worry that companies will choose cheap machine-made pictures over paying people, and that young artists will lose the chance to [[sharpen|L6-0803]] their skills through paid work.

Supporters see things differently. They point out that when photography first appeared, some people [[deemed|L6-0225]] it a threat to painting, yet painting survived. They argue that AI can [[enhance|L6-0305]] human creativity rather than replace it. It has even helped with [[restoration|L6-0761]] work: in 2021, a museum in Amsterdam used it to help recreate missing edges of Rembrandt's famous painting The Night Watch.

There are also legal questions. In the United States, officials have stated that a work made entirely by a machine, without enough human input, cannot be protected by copyright. In other words, the rights to a picture [[reside|L6-0758]] with a human creator, not with a program. Many countries are still deciding their rules, so it would be [[rash|L6-0726]] to assume the answers are settled.

Perhaps the best path is balance. An old [[proverb|L6-0707]] says that fire is a good servant but a bad master, and the same may be true of AI. Too much [[reliance|L6-0749]] on it could weaken our own creativity. But those who use it honestly, giving credit and respecting other people's work, are likely to [[reap|L6-0729]] its benefits without losing what makes art human.
zh: 2022 年，一張描繪宏偉發光大廳的圖像，在美國科羅拉多州的一場比賽中，贏得了數位藝術組的首獎。這幅畫充滿了壯麗之感，卻不是任何人親手畫出來的。創作者把文字描述輸入一個 AI 程式，再從生成的結果中挑出最好的一張。消息傳開後，有些藝術家為這些新的可能性感到欣喜，但也有許多人非常憤怒。隨之而來的爭論至今仍圍繞著一個問題：誰才是真正的藝術家？
AI 程式透過研究大量現有的圖像來學習，其中許多圖像出自從未被徵求同意的在世藝術家之手。之後，這些程式就能在幾秒內複製一位藝術家的風格。對一位花了多年時間才把畫筆練得純熟的畫家來說，這可能帶來真正的痛苦。也有人擔心，公司會選擇便宜的機器生成圖片，而不付錢請人創作；年輕的藝術家也會因此失去透過有酬工作來磨練技巧的機會。
支持者則有不同的看法。他們指出，攝影剛出現時，有些人認為它會威脅繪畫，但繪畫依然存活下來。他們主張，AI 能增強人類的創造力，而不是取代它。它甚至在修復工作上派上用場：2021 年，阿姆斯特丹的一間博物館就利用 AI 協助重現林布蘭名畫《夜巡》缺失的邊緣部分。
此外還有法律上的問題。在美國，官方已經表示，一件完全由機器製作、缺乏足夠人類參與的作品，無法受到著作權保護。換句話說，一幅畫的權利屬於人類創作者，而不屬於程式。許多國家仍在制定自己的規定，所以如果認定答案已經底定，未免太過輕率。
或許最好的方向是取得平衡。一句古老的諺語說，火是好僕人，卻是壞主人；AI 或許也是如此。過度依賴它，可能會削弱我們自身的創造力。但那些誠實使用它、註明出處並尊重他人作品的人，很可能既能收穫它帶來的好處，又不會失去讓藝術之所以為人類藝術的特質。

questions.stem: The word "reside" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 前一句說完全由機器製作的作品無法受著作權保護，接著用 In other words 換句話說：權利 reside with 人類創作者而非程式，也就是「屬於」人類，故選 (D)。

questions.stem: What is the writer's attitude toward AI art?

questions.explain: 作者在最後一段說最好的方向是取得平衡：過度依賴會削弱創造力，但誠實使用的人能收穫好處，可見態度持平，故選 (B)。(A)、(C) 都太極端，與「平衡」的結論不符。

title: The Painter of the Desert
paragraphs: Georgia O'Keeffe knew she wanted to be an artist before she was a teenager. Born in 1887 on a farm in Wisconsin, she studied art in Chicago and New York, where students were taught to copy great painters of the past. Over time, O'Keeffe grew [[weary|L6-0987]] of painting the way others told her to and of [[suppressing|L6-0890]] her own ideas. In 1915, while working as an art teacher, she put away her colors and began making simple drawings in black charcoal, using lines and shapes that came from her own feelings.

These drawings were pure [[abstraction|L6-0005]]: they showed no people, places, or objects. A friend showed some of them to Alfred Stieglitz, a [[renowned|L6-0754]] photographer who ran an art gallery in New York, and in 1916 he displayed them to the public. [[Acclaim|L6-0009]] soon followed, and within a few years, O'Keeffe had become one of the best-known artists in America.

In the 1920s, she became famous for huge paintings of flowers, painted as if seen through a [[magnifying|L6-0535]] glass. She explained that busy New Yorkers would hurry past a small flower. She wanted them to stop and look, and she painted [[accordingly|L6-0011]]: her flowers filled the whole picture. Critics, however, claimed that the flowers had hidden meanings about her life as a woman. O'Keeffe rejected these [[subjective|L6-0875]] readings, saying the critics were describing their own thoughts, not hers.

In 1929, she visited New Mexico for the first time, and the desert changed her work forever. Red hills and wide skies [[abound|L6-0004]] there, and she was drawn to its [[abundance|L6-0006]] of color and light. On long walks, she collected bones that the sun had turned white, and her growing [[accumulation|L6-0014]] of bones soon appeared in her paintings, sometimes floating in the sky above [[majestic|L6-0538]] hills. After 1949, she lived in New Mexico full-time.

In 1946, the Museum of Modern Art in New York held a major show of her work, its first for a woman. She died in 1986 at the age of 98. Today, her paintings still [[transmit|L6-0925]] the quiet power she felt in the open desert.
zh: 喬治亞・歐姬芙在還沒進入青少年時期之前，就知道自己想當藝術家。她 1887 年出生於美國威斯康辛州的一座農場，後來在芝加哥和紐約學習藝術，那裡的學生被教導要臨摹過去的偉大畫家。久而久之，歐姬芙厭倦了照著別人的方式作畫，也厭倦了壓抑自己的想法。1915 年，她一邊擔任美術老師，一邊把顏料收起來，開始用黑色炭筆畫簡單的素描，畫中的線條和形狀都來自她自己的感受。
這些素描是純粹的抽象作品：畫中沒有人物、地點或物體。一位朋友把其中幾幅拿給亞弗烈・史蒂格利茲看，他是一位知名的攝影師，在紐約經營一間藝廊；1916 年，他把這些作品公開展出。讚譽很快隨之而來，短短幾年內，歐姬芙就成為美國最知名的藝術家之一。
1920 年代，她以巨大的花卉畫作聞名，畫中的花朵就像透過放大鏡看到的一樣。她解釋說，忙碌的紐約人會匆匆走過一朵小花。她希望讓他們停下腳步好好看，並依此作畫：她筆下的花朵占滿了整幅畫面。然而，評論家宣稱這些花朵暗藏著與她身為女性的生活有關的意義。歐姬芙拒絕接受這些主觀的解讀，她說評論家描述的是他們自己的想法，而不是她的。
1929 年，她第一次造訪新墨西哥州，那裡的沙漠從此改變了她的作品。那裡到處是紅色的山丘和遼闊的天空，豐富的色彩與光線深深吸引著她。在長途散步時，她撿拾被太陽曬白的骨頭，而她越收越多的骨頭很快就出現在畫作中，有時就飄浮在雄偉山丘上方的天空裡。1949 年之後，她便長住在新墨西哥州。
1946 年，紐約現代藝術博物館為她舉辦了一場大型展覽，這是該館首次為女性藝術家舉辦的大型展覽。她於 1986 年過世，享年 98 歲。時至今日，她的畫作仍傳達出她在開闊沙漠中感受到的那股寧靜力量。

title: A Proposal for Phone-Free Lunch Fridays
paragraphs: Dear Principal Chen and Members of the [[Advisory|L6-0024]] Committee,

We are writing to propose a simple change: every Friday, students would put their phones away during lunch, from 12:10 to 12:50. [[Amid|L6-0039]] our busy school weeks, lunch is one of the few times we can relax together. Yet in many classrooms, the only sound at lunch is the quiet tapping of fingers on screens. Ringing phones are also a common source of [[annoyance|L6-0045]].

[[Adolescence|L6-0023]] is a time when friendships matter deeply, but many of us have become so [[accustomed|L6-0016]] to looking at our phones that we rarely talk to the people beside us. Some students even worry that their phone use is turning into an [[addiction|L6-0020]]. Last month, we [[administered|L6-0021]] a short survey to students in all three grades. Most of those who answered said they would like to spend less time on their phones at school, and many said they sometimes feel [[alienated|L6-0032]] from classmates whose eyes never leave their screens.

To avoid any [[ambiguity|L6-0038]], here is how the plan would work. Phones would stay in students' bags, not on desks. Students could still use them in an emergency or with a teacher's permission. In place of screens, the council would provide board games, a music corner, and paper for drawing. Several teachers have already [[affirmed|L6-0028]] their support, and any teacher who wishes to join us is warmly invited.

We believe this plan [[aligns|L6-0033]] with our school's goal of building a caring community and would [[enrich|L6-0307]] our school life. It is not meant as an [[accusation|L6-0015]] against students who enjoy their phones, and no one would be punished. We simply hope to [[amplify|L6-0040]] the sound of real conversation and [[nurture|L6-0597]] friendships. If the committee agrees, we suggest a six-week trial, after which we would collect feedback and adjust the plan [[accordingly|L6-0011]]. Amy Lin, our [[chairperson|L6-0138]], would be glad to present the plan at your next meeting. Thank you for considering our proposal.

Sincerely,
The Student Council
zh: 敬愛的陳校長暨諮詢委員會各位委員：
我們寫這封信，是想提議一項簡單的改變：每週五午餐時間，從 12:10 到 12:50，學生把手機收起來。在忙碌的校園生活中，午餐是我們少數能一起放鬆的時光。然而在許多教室裡，午餐時唯一的聲音卻是手指輕敲螢幕的聲響。此起彼落的手機鈴聲，也常常令人感到惱怒。
青春期是友誼格外重要的階段，但我們之中有許多人已經太習慣盯著手機，很少和身邊的人說話。有些同學甚至擔心自己使用手機的情況正逐漸變成上癮。上個月，我們對三個年級的學生進行了一份簡短的問卷調查。大多數填答的同學表示，希望在學校少花一點時間在手機上；也有許多人說，面對眼睛從不離開螢幕的同學，有時會覺得彼此疏遠。
為避免任何模稜兩可之處，以下說明這項計畫的實施方式：手機放在學生的書包裡，不放在桌上。遇到緊急情況，或經老師允許，學生仍然可以使用手機。學生會將提供桌遊、音樂角落和繪畫用紙來取代螢幕。已有幾位老師表態支持，也誠摯歡迎任何有意參加的老師加入我們。
我們相信，這項計畫符合學校建立關懷社群的目標，也能讓我們的校園生活更加豐富。這項提議並不是要指責喜歡使用手機的同學，也不會處罰任何人。我們只是希望讓真實對話的聲音更響亮，並培養彼此的友誼。如果委員會同意，我們建議先試行六週，之後蒐集意見回饋，並據此調整計畫。我們的主席林艾美很樂意在您下次的會議中說明這項計畫。感謝您考慮我們的提案。
學生會　敬上
