vocab.stem: The singer had shouted so much at the concert that her voice was ______ the next morning.
vocab.explain: 演唱會上喊得太用力，隔天早上聲音變得「沙啞」，故選 hoarse。honorary（榮譽的）、hybrid（混合的）、healthful（有益健康的）都不能說明喊太多後聲音的狀態。

vocab.stem: The traveler stayed in a cheap ______, where she shared a room with five other young people.
vocab.explain: 價格便宜、和其他五個年輕人同住一間房的住宿地點是「青年旅館」，故選 hostel。harmonica（口琴）、hierarchy（階級制度）、hedge（樹籬）都不是可以住宿的地方。

title: The Cow That Changed Medicine
paragraphs: For centuries, smallpox was one of the most feared [[infectious|L6-0447]] diseases on Earth. It was [[transmitted|L6-0925]] easily from person to person, [[inflicted|L6-0449]] terrible pain, and left many survivors with deep scars or without their sight. In some cities, it killed a large share of the [[inhabitants|L6-0451]], and over the centuries it took [[innumerable|L6-0454]] lives, from poor farmers to kings.

People noticed early that those who survived smallpox never caught it again. In China, India, and other places, healthy people were given a small amount of material from a sick person, either through the nose or through a tiny cut in the skin. This usually caused a milder case of the disease that left them protected. The method was risky, but when an [[outbreak|L6-0622]] seemed [[imminent|L6-0434]], many parents' [[instinctive|L6-0457]] fear of the disease made them willing to try it.

The next step came from England. Doctor Edward Jenner had heard that women who milked cows and caught cowpox, a mild disease, seemed to be safe from smallpox. In 1796, he took material from a cowpox sore on a woman's hand and placed it in a small cut on the arm of an eight-year-old boy. Weeks later, Jenner exposed the boy to smallpox, and the boy did not become sick. The word "[[vaccine|L6-0955]]" comes from the Latin word for cow.

Not everyone welcomed the new idea. Some people were [[indignant|L6-0444]] at the thought of putting material from animals into human bodies, and one famous cartoon showed people growing parts of cows after being treated. Jenner answered them with his [[insistence|L6-0456]] on evidence. He kept collecting cases, and doctors from many countries wrote to [[inquire|L6-0455]] about his method.

In the following decades, the method spread around the world. Then, in the 1960s and 1970s, health workers searched for every last case of smallpox. In 1980, the World Health Organization announced that the disease was gone. The story shows that protecting public health is [[imperative|L6-0435]], and that [[indifference|L6-0443]] can be costly.
zh: 幾百年來，天花一直是地球上最令人恐懼的傳染病之一。它很容易在人與人之間傳播，會帶來劇烈的痛苦，許多倖存者留下很深的疤痕，甚至失明。在某些城市，天花奪走了很大比例居民的性命；幾個世紀以來，它奪走了無數人的生命，從貧窮的農夫到國王都無法倖免。
人們很早就發現，得過天花而活下來的人不會再被傳染。在中國、印度等地，人們會讓健康的人接觸少量來自病人的物質，方法是從鼻子吸入，或是放進皮膚上的小傷口。這通常會引起較輕微的病症，之後這個人就受到保護。這種做法有風險，但當疫情似乎即將爆發時，許多父母出於對這種疾病本能的恐懼，願意一試。
下一步發生在英國。愛德華・詹納醫生聽說，替乳牛擠奶而感染牛痘（一種輕微疾病）的婦女，似乎不會得天花。1796 年，他從一名婦女手上的牛痘傷處取出物質，放進一名八歲男孩手臂上的小傷口。幾週後，詹納讓這個男孩接觸天花，男孩並沒有生病。「疫苗」（vaccine）這個字就是源自拉丁文的「牛」。
並不是每個人都歡迎這個新觀念。有些人一想到要把來自動物的物質放進人體就憤憤不平，一幅有名的漫畫甚至畫出人們接種後身上長出牛的部位。詹納則以堅持證據來回應他們。他持續蒐集病例，許多國家的醫生也寫信來詢問他的方法。
在接下來的幾十年間，這種方法傳遍了全世界。到了 1960 和 1970 年代，醫療人員四處搜尋每一個殘存的天花病例。1980 年，世界衛生組織宣布天花已經絕跡。這段歷史告訴我們，保護公共衛生是刻不容緩的事，而漠不關心可能要付出很大的代價。

questions.stem: What did people in places like China and India do to protect themselves from smallpox?
options: They used medicine made from plants.
They kept all sick people far away from cities.
They gave healthy people a small amount of material from a sick person.
questions.explain: 第二段說在中國、印度等地，人們讓健康的人經由鼻子或皮膚小傷口接觸少量病人的物質，引起較輕微的病症而得到保護，故選 (D)。(A) 擠牛奶的婦女是第三段詹納故事的內容。
questions.evidence: healthy people were given a small amount of material from a sick person

questions.stem: What did Jenner do in 1796?
options: He caught cowpox from a cow himself.
He placed cowpox material in a small cut on a boy's arm.
He drew a famous cartoon about cows.
He announced that smallpox was gone.
questions.explain: 第三段說 1796 年詹納從婦女手上的牛痘傷處取出物質，放進一名八歲男孩手臂上的小傷口，故選 (B)。(C) 漫畫是反對者畫的，(D) 宣布天花絕跡的是 1980 年的世界衛生組織。
questions.evidence: placed it in a small cut on the arm of an eight-year-old boy

questions.stem: The word "indignant" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
options: angry about something that seems wrong
questions.explain: 這些人不歡迎新觀念，一想到要把動物的物質放進人體就 indignant，還有漫畫加以嘲諷，可知是「憤慨的、覺得不對而生氣的」，故選 (C)。(B) 與「不歡迎」的態度相反。
questions.evidence: Some people were indignant at the thought of putting material from animals into human bodies

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the last paragraph?
options: Ending smallpox took a long, worldwide effort.
Jenner himself searched for every last case.
Vaccines are no longer needed for any disease.
Smallpox still kills many people today.
questions.explain: 最後一段說方法在數十年間傳遍全球，1960、70 年代醫療人員還要搜尋每一個殘存病例，直到 1980 年才宣布絕跡，可推知消滅天花是長期且全球性的努力，故選 (A)。(D) 與天花已絕跡的事實矛盾。
questions.evidence: health workers searched for every last case of smallpox

vocab.stem: In the late 1700s, Britain began to ______ quickly, and many farmers moved to cities to work in factories.
vocab.explain: 許多農民搬到城市的工廠工作，表示英國開始快速「工業化」，故選 industrialize。inquire（詢問）、intervene（介入）、inflict（施加痛苦）都無法說明農民為何改到工廠工作。

vocab.stem: To stay healthy, doctors suggest that we watch our daily sugar ______ and drink more water.
vocab.explain: 為了健康要注意每天糖分的「攝取量」，sugar intake 是常見搭配，故選 intake。interpreter（口譯員）、insistence（堅持）、intellect（智力）都不能和 sugar 搭配表示吃進去的量。

title: The Fortune Teller at the Corner
paragraphs: The night market was loud and [[jolly|L6-0483]]. The smell of grilled corn filled the air, children laughed, and a [[lad|L6-0489]] at a drink stand shouted prices over the noise. Pei-shan, who was seventeen, had come only because her cousin Min insisted. Weeks of [[cramming|L6-0204]] for the exam had made her [[irritable|L6-0473]], and even the happy crowd seemed to [[irritate|L6-0474]] her.

At the [[junction|L6-0485]] of two narrow lanes sat an old woman behind a small table. A sign read "Your Future: 100 Dollars." She wore a [[jade|L6-0478]] bracelet, and the smell of her [[jasmine|L6-0480]] tea [[lingered|L6-0510]] in the air around her. Her sharp eyes [[intimidated|L6-0464]] Pei-shan at first, but she was also [[intrigued|L6-0466]]. "Go on," Min said. "Ask her about the exam."

The woman did not ask to see Pei-shan's hand. Instead, she pushed a cup of bamboo sticks across the table and asked her to pick one. Then she asked a few simple questions. When did Pei-shan go to bed? What did she do when a problem seemed too hard? Her [[intonation|L6-0465]] was calm and slow, like a teacher reading a story aloud. Finally she said, "Your future is bright, but only if you sleep before midnight and study one subject at a time."

Pei-shan laughed. "That's not a fortune. That's advice!" The woman smiled. "People [[invariably|L6-0470]] say that," she replied. "For thirty years I taught math at the high school down the road. My students never listened to my advice in class, but now they pay me to hear it." Pei-shan could not stop laughing at how [[ironic|L6-0472]] it was, though she was still [[dubious|L6-0286]] about the bamboo sticks.

Walking home, Pei-shan realized that the old teacher had [[kindled|L6-0487]] something in her: not magic, but hope. She followed the advice for the next month. When her test results slowly improved, she knew the stick she had picked meant nothing. The words, however, had been [[invaluable|L6-0469]].
zh: 夜市又吵又熱鬧。烤玉米的香味瀰漫在空氣中，孩子們笑著，飲料攤的一個少年扯著嗓子在喧鬧聲中喊價錢。十七歲的佩珊會來，只是因為表姊阿敏一再堅持。為了考試死命苦讀了好幾個星期，她變得很容易煩躁，連歡樂的人潮似乎都讓她心煩。
在兩條窄巷交會的路口，一位老婦人坐在一張小桌子後面。招牌上寫著：「你的未來：100 元。」她戴著一只玉鐲，茉莉花茶的香氣在她身邊久久不散。她銳利的目光一開始讓佩珊有點害怕，卻也勾起了她的好奇心。「去啊，」阿敏說，「問問她考試的事。」
老婦人沒有要看佩珊的手，而是把一杯竹籤推過桌面，請她抽一支。接著，她問了幾個簡單的問題：佩珊幾點上床睡覺？遇到太難的題目時她會怎麼做？她的語調平穩而緩慢，就像老師在朗讀故事。最後她說：「妳的未來很光明，但前提是妳要在午夜前睡覺，而且一次只讀一個科目。」
佩珊笑了出來：「這不是算命，這是建議吧！」老婦人微笑著回答：「大家總是這麼說。我在這條路上的那所高中教了三十年數學。學生上課時從來不聽我的建議，現在倒是付錢來聽。」佩珊忍不住一直笑，覺得這實在太諷刺了，不過她對那些竹籤還是半信半疑。
走路回家時，佩珊發現這位退休老師在她心中點燃了某種東西：不是魔法，而是希望。接下來一個月，她照著那些建議去做。當她的考試成績慢慢進步時，她知道自己抽到的那支籤其實沒有任何意義。然而，那番話卻是無價的。

questions.stem: Why did Pei-shan go to the night market?
options: Her cousin Min insisted that she come.
She wanted to have her fortune told.
She wanted to buy jasmine tea.
She worked at a drink stand there.
questions.explain: 第一段說佩珊會去夜市，只是因為表姊阿敏一再堅持，故選 (A)。(B) 是阿敏到了夜市才鼓勵她去問的，並不是她去的原因。
questions.evidence: had come only because her cousin Min insisted

questions.stem: What did the old woman do before she told Pei-shan her "future"?
options: She looked closely at Pei-shan's hand.
She had Pei-shan pick a stick and asked about her habits.
She poured Pei-shan a cup of jasmine tea.
questions.explain: 第三段說老婦人沒有看手，而是請佩珊抽一支竹籤，接著問她幾點睡、遇到難題怎麼辦等問題，故選 (C)。(A) 文中明確說她沒有要看佩珊的手。
questions.evidence: Then she asked a few simple questions.

questions.stem: The word "ironic" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
options: funny because the opposite of what you expect happens
questions.explain: 學生上課時免費聽建議卻不聽，現在反而付錢來聽同樣的建議，結果與預期相反，讓佩珊忍不住發笑，所以 ironic 指「諷刺的」，故選 (D)。(B) 與佩珊大笑的反應不符。
questions.evidence: Pei-shan could not stop laughing at how ironic it was

questions.stem: What most likely helped Pei-shan improve her test results?
options: The lucky bamboo stick she picked
Following the old woman's practical advice
questions.explain: 最後一段說她照著建議做了一個月，成績慢慢進步，並明白抽到的籤沒有意義，真正無價的是那番話，故選 (B)。(A) 正是她認為沒有意義的東西，(C) 與「午夜前睡覺」的建議相反。
questions.evidence: she knew the stick she had picked meant nothing

vocab.stem: The shop owner checked her ______ and found that only three boxes of tea were left.
vocab.explain: 店主檢查後發現茶只剩三盒，她查看的是「存貨」，故選 inventory。intimacy（親密）、intonation（語調）無法查出貨物數量；janitor（工友）是人，不能用來「查到剩幾盒茶」。

vocab.stem: Living on a small ______ far out in the sea, the children have to take a boat to school.
vocab.explain: 住在遠離陸地的海上、要搭船上學，表示住在一座「小島」上，故選 isle。ivy（常春藤）、landlady（女房東）都不是可以居住的地方，junction（交叉路口）不會位於海上。

title: Research Summary: Lighter Bags, Healthier Backs
paragraphs:
Research Summary
Greenfield Institute of Child Health
Project: Heavy School Bags and Student Health

Background: Many students carry heavy bags every day, filled with textbooks, a computer, and a one-[[liter|L6-0512]] water bottle. Earlier studies have suggested that carrying too much weight may make young people more [[liable|L6-0502]] to back and shoulder pain. Our team wanted to find out whether simple changes at school could [[lighten|L6-0507]] this load.

Method: For the [[duration|L6-0287]] of one school year, we followed 240 students aged 13 to 16 at two schools. At School A, every student was given a free [[locker|L6-0518]], and teachers kept copies of the heaviest textbooks in their classrooms. School B made no changes. Once a month, all of the students weighed their bags and answered a short survey about pain. Unlike a [[lengthy|L6-0498]] interview, the survey took only five minutes, and we [[compiled|L6-0168]] the answers at the end of each term.

Results: By the end of the year, bags at School A weighed [[approximately|L6-0053]] 40 percent less than before, while bags at School B did not change. Students at School A also reported less back pain. A few who had walked with a slight [[limp|L6-0508]] after long days of carrying heavy bags said the problem had disappeared. Several told us that a weight had been lifted off their shoulders, in the most [[literal|L6-0514]] sense.

What this means: In [[layman's|L6-0494]] terms, a lighter bag means a happier back. We recommend that schools provide lockers wherever possible, and that families choose bags with two wide straps and a soft [[lining|L6-0511]]. These changes need not be [[lavish|L6-0493]]; even small steps can [[lessen|L6-0500]] pain. Since habits formed in youth can become [[lifelong|L6-0506]], protecting students' backs now may help them for years to come. A more [[comprehensive|L6-0171]] study, with schools in three cities, is planned for next year.
zh:
研究摘要
綠野兒童健康研究所
研究計畫：沉重書包與學生健康
研究背景：許多學生每天背著沉重的書包，裡面裝滿課本、一台電腦和一瓶一公升的水。先前的研究指出，背負過重可能讓年輕人更容易背痛和肩膀痛。我們的團隊想了解，學校做一些簡單的改變，是否就能減輕這份負擔。
研究方法：在一整個學年期間，我們追蹤了兩所學校中 240 名 13 到 16 歲的學生。A 校為每位學生提供免費的置物櫃，老師也在教室裡放置最重課本的備用本；B 校則沒有做任何改變。每個月，所有學生都會量自己書包的重量，並填寫一份關於疼痛的簡短問卷。我們不採用冗長的訪談，問卷只需五分鐘就能完成，並在每學期末彙整回答。
研究結果：到了學年末，A 校學生的書包重量比原本減輕了大約 40%，B 校學生的書包重量則沒有改變。A 校學生回報的背痛也比較少。少數原本在背了一整天重書包後走路會微跛的學生表示，這個問題已經消失了。好幾位學生告訴我們，他們肩上的重擔真的、名副其實地被卸下了。
研究意涵：用一般人聽得懂的話來說，書包越輕，背就越健康。我們建議學校盡可能提供置物櫃，家長則選擇有兩條寬背帶和柔軟內襯的書包。這些改變不需要花大錢，即使是小小的措施也能減輕疼痛。由於年輕時養成的習慣可能伴隨一生，現在保護學生的背，可能讓他們在未來許多年都受益。明年我們將進行一項涵蓋三個城市學校、更全面的研究。

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of this text?
options: To sell a new kind of school bag
To report a study on heavy school bags and suggest changes
To invite students to join a study next year
To explain how students should use lockers
questions.explain: 本文是研究摘要，依序說明研究背景、方法、結果與建議，主旨在報告書包重量的研究並提出改善建議，故選 (B)。(C) 文末只提到明年將有更全面的研究，並沒有邀請學生參加。
questions.evidence: Our team wanted to find out whether simple changes at school could lighten this load.

questions.stem: What did School A do that School B did not do?
options: It gave every student a free locker and kept copies of heavy textbooks in classrooms.
It asked every student to buy a new bag.
It made the school day shorter.
It held lengthy interviews with students.
questions.explain: 研究方法一段說 A 校提供免費置物櫃，老師也在教室放置最重課本的備用本，而 B 校沒有任何改變，故選 (A)。(D) 文中說研究不採用冗長的訪談。
questions.evidence: At School A, every student was given a free locker

questions.stem: According to the results, what happened at School A?
options: Bags weighed approximately 40 percent less than before.
questions.explain: 研究結果一段說學年末 A 校的書包重量比原本減輕約 40%，學生回報的背痛也比較少，故選 (C)。(B) 與「背痛較少」的結果相反。
questions.evidence: bags at School A weighed approximately 40 percent less than before

questions.stem: The phrase "in layman's terms" in the last paragraph is closest in meaning to ______.
options: in a short period of time
in simple words that most people can understand
questions.explain: 這句話後面接的是「書包越輕，背就越健康」這種人人都懂的簡單說法，可知 in layman's terms 是「用一般人聽得懂的話來說」，故選 (D)。(B) 醫生的專業用語正好相反。
questions.evidence: In layman's terms, a lighter bag means a happier back.

vocab.stem: Some snakes carry a ______ poison that can kill a person within a few hours.
vocab.explain: 能在幾小時內致人於死的毒液是「致命的」，故選 lethal。lofty（崇高的）、lavish（奢華的）、lengthy（冗長的）都不能用來形容會害死人的毒液。

vocab.stem: Heavy rain caused a ______ that blocked the mountain road for three days.
vocab.explain: 大雨造成某種事情，使山路封閉三天，最合理的是「山崩」，故選 landslide。lease（租約）、liner（郵輪；內襯）、lieutenant（中尉）都不是大雨造成、會擋住山路的東西。

title: The Boy Who Played at the Palace
paragraphs: In 1762, a six-year-old boy from Salzburg sat down at a keyboard in a palace in Vienna and played for Her [[Majesty|L6-0539]] Maria Theresa, the ruler of Austria. The boy was Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and the trip was one of many tours that his father, Leopold, planned for him and his older sister, Nannerl. Audiences across Europe [[marveled|L6-0545]] at a child who could play difficult music with a cloth over the keys and write his own pieces at an age when most children were still learning to read.

His [[mastery|L6-0546]] of music grew quickly. By his teens he had written symphonies and operas, and the [[manuscripts|L6-0540]] of his works filled box after box. Yet life back home in Salzburg was often [[lonesome|L6-0522]] and frustrating. He worked for the ruler of the city, a job that was not [[lucrative|L6-0529]] and gave him little freedom. The young composer was treated almost like a servant and given only a [[marginal|L6-0543]] place at court.

In 1781, the [[lure|L6-0532]] of Vienna, with its theaters and wealthy music lovers, proved too strong. Mozart left his job and moved to the capital. There he tried to earn a living mainly on his own, without a steady position at court. He gave concerts, taught students, and sold his music. Some years went well; others left him deep in debt. Still, the music kept coming: piano music, church music, and operas such as The Marriage of Figaro and The Magic Flute, which were [[applauded|L6-0050]] by large crowds.

Mozart did not enjoy [[longevity|L6-0523]]. He died in 1791 at the age of 35, before he could finish his Requiem, a piece of music for the dead. Listeners often hear a [[melancholy|L6-0551]] tone in some of his later works, though much of his music remains bright and playful. More than 600 of his works survive from a career that [[spanned|L6-0843]] only about thirty years, and people still [[meditate|L6-0549]] on how one short life could produce so much. Today this [[renowned|L6-0754]] composer's music fills concert halls and films, and it even plays from [[loudspeakers|L6-0528]] in train stations and shops.
zh: 1762 年，一個來自薩爾斯堡的六歲男孩，在維也納的一座宮殿裡坐到鍵盤樂器前，為奧地利的統治者瑪麗亞・特蕾莎女王陛下演奏。這個男孩就是沃夫岡・阿瑪迪斯・莫札特；這趟旅程是他父親李奧波德為他和姊姊南妮兒安排的多次巡迴演出之一。歐洲各地的聽眾都對這個孩子驚嘆不已：他能在琴鍵蓋上一塊布的情況下彈奏艱難的樂曲，而且在大多數孩子還在學認字的年紀，就已經會自己作曲。
他對音樂的精通程度進步得很快。十幾歲時，他已經寫出交響曲和歌劇，作品的手稿裝滿了一箱又一箱。然而，回到薩爾斯堡家鄉的生活卻常常孤單又令人沮喪。他替這座城市的統治者工作，這份工作收入不豐，也讓他沒什麼自由。這位年輕的作曲家幾乎被當作僕人看待，在宮廷中只占有邊緣的位置。
1781 年，擁有眾多劇院和富裕樂迷的維也納，吸引力實在太強了。莫札特辭去工作，搬到了首都。在那裡，他嘗試大多靠自己謀生，沒有在宮廷擔任穩定的職位。他開音樂會、教學生，也出售自己的樂譜。有些年過得不錯，有些年卻讓他負債累累。儘管如此，音樂仍源源不絕地誕生：鋼琴作品、教會音樂，以及《費加洛婚禮》、《魔笛》等歌劇，這些作品都獲得大批觀眾的喝采。
莫札特並不長壽。他在 1791 年過世，年僅 35 歲，來不及完成他的《安魂曲》——一首為亡者所寫的樂曲。聽眾常在他晚期的某些作品中聽到憂鬱的情調，不過他大部分的音樂依然明亮而活潑。他的音樂生涯只橫跨大約三十年，卻有六百多部作品流傳下來，人們至今仍在沉思：這麼短暫的一生，怎麼能創作出這麼多作品？如今，這位知名作曲家的音樂充滿音樂廳與電影，甚至在火車站和商店的擴音器裡播放。

questions.stem: What amazed audiences about the young Mozart?
options: He had traveled to more countries than any other child.
He could play with the keys covered and write his own music.
He had written an opera for Maria Theresa.
He was taught by the best teachers in Vienna.
questions.explain: 第一段說歐洲聽眾驚嘆於這個孩子能在琴鍵蓋上布的情況下彈奏艱難樂曲，還能在多數孩子剛學認字的年紀自己作曲，故選 (B)。(C) 文中沒有提到他為瑪麗亞・特蕾莎寫歌劇。
questions.evidence: a child who could play difficult music with a cloth over the keys

questions.stem: Why was Mozart unhappy with his job in Salzburg?
options: It paid poorly and gave him little freedom.
He could not find any students there.
Audiences there did not like operas.
His sister had already moved to Vienna.
questions.explain: 第二段說他在薩爾斯堡替統治者工作，收入不豐又沒什麼自由，還被當成僕人看待，故選 (A)。(C)、(D) 文中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: a job that was not lucrative and gave him little freedom

questions.stem: The word "lure" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 維也納有眾多劇院和富裕的樂迷，它的 lure「太強」，讓莫札特辭職搬過去，可知 lure 指「誘惑；吸引力」，故選 (C)。(A) 沉重的責任與他主動前往的情境不合。
questions.evidence: the lure of Vienna, with its theaters and wealthy music lovers, proved too strong

questions.stem: What can be inferred about Mozart's life in Vienna?
options: He finally received a large salary from the emperor.
He stopped writing music so that he could focus on teaching.
He spent most of his time touring Europe with his family.
His income went up and down from year to year.
questions.explain: 第三段說他靠開音樂會、教學生、賣樂譜謀生，有些年過得不錯，有些年卻負債累累，可推知他的收入並不穩定，故選 (D)。(B) 與「音樂仍源源不絕」的敘述相反。
questions.evidence: Some years went well; others left him deep in debt.

vocab.stem: The doctor told me to put this ______ on my dry skin twice a day.
vocab.explain: 可以每天兩次擦在乾燥皮膚上的是「乳液」，故選 lotion。logo（標誌）、lotus（蓮花）、lottery（樂透彩券）都不能擦在皮膚上。

vocab.stem: After the spring rains, the hills were covered in ______ green grass.
vocab.explain: 春雨過後，山坡上長滿了「茂盛的」青草，故選 lush。lunar（月亮的）、martial（軍事的；武術的）、lucrative（賺錢的）都不能用來形容草。

title: Notes from the Lamp Room
paragraphs: March 3, 1894. The supply boat left this morning, and I am alone again on this small [[isle|L6-0475]]. Its only other [[inhabitants|L6-0451]] are the [[innumerable|L6-0454]] birds that [[hover|L6-0425]] above the rocks all day. My father kept this light before me, and I suppose it will be my work for the rest of my life. Tonight I cleaned the great glass lens and lit the lamp. Watching its beam [[illuminate|L6-0433]] the dark water, I felt a little less [[lonesome|L6-0522]].

March 9. A [[lengthy|L6-0498]] storm: three days and nights without rest. My voice is [[hoarse|L6-0418]] from singing to stay awake, and I have grown [[irritable|L6-0473]] because I am so tired. Still, I [[invariably|L6-0470]] climb the stairs every four hours to wind the machine that turns the light. If the light stopped, a ship could strike the rocks, and that thought is enough to keep me going.

March 15. Calm at last. The [[lunar|L6-0531]] light was so bright tonight that the sea looked silver. Around midnight, however, I had a [[hunch|L6-0427]] that something was wrong. A thick fog was rolling in, and I could hear a ship's horn somewhere to the south. With an almost [[instinctive|L6-0457]] movement, I began ringing the fog bell, and I kept ringing it for two hours. At dawn a fishing boat came slowly into our little bay, its crew safe. Their captain, a cheerful old man, waved his cap and gave a [[hearty|L6-0409]] laugh that [[lightened|L6-0507]] my mood for the whole day. I made them hot tea, and they [[lingered|L6-0510]] by my fire for an hour before sailing home.

March 20. In the evenings I have been reading the old notebooks left by the keepers before me. Some are full of missing home; others describe whales, strange lights, and the joy of the first spring flowers. Their words are [[invaluable|L6-0469]] company. Though we never met, each of us faced the same long nights and the same wild sea.

March 21. I often sit by the lamp and [[meditate|L6-0549]] on why I stay in this lonely place. Tonight the answer seems simple. Somewhere out there, a sailor is searching the dark for this light. As long as I keep it burning, no one has to feel lost.
zh: 1894 年 3 月 3 日。補給船今天早上離開了，我又獨自一人留在這座小島上。島上僅有的其他居民，是整天在岩石上方盤旋、數也數不清的鳥。我父親在我之前看守這座燈塔，我想這也會是我一輩子的工作。今晚我擦亮了巨大的玻璃透鏡，點亮了燈。看著光束照亮漆黑的海面，我覺得沒那麼孤單了。
3 月 9 日。一場漫長的暴風雨：三天三夜沒有休息。我為了保持清醒一直唱歌，唱到聲音都沙啞了，也因為太累而變得容易發脾氣。儘管如此，我總是每四個小時就爬上樓梯，為轉動燈光的機器上發條。要是燈光停了，船隻可能會撞上岩石；光是這個念頭就足以讓我撐下去。
3 月 15 日。終於風平浪靜了。今晚的月光亮得讓海面看起來一片銀白。然而到了半夜，我直覺有什麼不對勁。濃霧正滾滾而來，我聽見南方某處傳來船的汽笛聲。我幾乎出於本能地開始敲響霧鐘，一連敲了兩個小時。天亮時，一艘漁船緩緩駛進我們的小海灣，船員都平安無事。他們的船長是位開朗的老人，揮著帽子發出爽朗的笑聲，讓我一整天心情都輕鬆起來。我為他們煮了熱茶，他們在我的爐火旁待了一個小時才啟航回家。
3 月 20 日。這幾個晚上，我一直在讀前幾任看守人留下的舊筆記本。有些寫滿了對家鄉的思念；有些則描述了鯨魚、奇怪的光，以及春天第一批花朵帶來的喜悅。他們的文字是無比珍貴的陪伴。雖然我們從未見過面，但我們每個人都面對著同樣漫長的夜晚，和同樣狂暴的大海。
3 月 21 日。我常坐在燈旁，沉思自己為什麼要留在這個孤寂的地方。今晚，答案似乎很簡單。在外面的某個地方，有一位水手正在黑暗中尋找這道光。只要我讓它一直亮著，就沒有人會感到迷失。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A keeper's life at a lonely lighthouse and why he stays there
The history of lighthouses around the world
How a fishing boat was lost in a storm
A keeper's plan to leave the island and return home
questions.explain: 這篇日記記錄燈塔看守人獨自守島、熬過暴風雨、在霧中敲鐘救船的生活，最後一則寫他思考自己為何留下，故選 (A)。(C) 漁船最後平安進港，並沒有失蹤。
questions.evidence: I often sit by the lamp and meditate on why I stay in this lonely place.

questions.stem: What did the writer do when the fog came in on March 15?
options: He lit a fire on the beach.
He took a boat out to find the ship.
He sent a message to the mainland.
He rang the fog bell for two hours.
questions.explain: 3 月 15 日的日記說，濃霧來時他幾乎出於本能地敲響霧鐘，一連敲了兩個小時，故選 (D)。其他選項文中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: I began ringing the fog bell, and I kept ringing it for two hours

questions.stem: Why does the writer call the old notebooks "invaluable company"?
options: They teach him how to repair the light.
They contain maps of the dangerous rocks.
They make him feel connected to keepers who lived the same life.
They were written by famous writers.
questions.explain: 他說雖然從未和前任看守人見過面，但大家都面對同樣漫長的夜晚和同樣的大海，可知這些筆記讓他感到和過去的看守人有所連結、不再孤單，故選 (C)。(A)、(B) 文中沒有提到筆記有修理方法或地圖。
questions.evidence: Though we never met, each of us faced the same long nights and the same wild sea.

questions.stem: The word "invariably" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 即使暴風雨中又累又煩躁，他仍 invariably 每四小時爬上樓梯，因為燈一停船就可能撞上岩石，可知是「總是、一定」這麼做，故選 (A)。(B) rarely（很少）與他堅持不懈的態度相反。
questions.evidence: I invariably climb the stairs every four hours to wind the machine that turns the light

vocab.stem: Selling fresh fruit at the night market turned out to be a ______ business; she earned enough to buy a car in two years.
vocab.explain: 兩年內就賺到足夠買車的錢，表示這是一門「很賺錢的」生意，故選 lucrative。martial（軍事的）、lunar（月亮的）、lush（茂盛的）都不能形容生意。

vocab.stem: Every morning, my grandfather sits quietly in the garden for twenty minutes of ______ to calm his mind.
vocab.explain: 每天早上安靜坐在花園裡二十分鐘來讓心平靜，是在「冥想」，故選 meditation。longitude（經度）、manuscript（手稿）、loudspeaker（擴音器）都無法讓人靜心。

title: What Happens When We Dream?
paragraphs: You are being chased by a [[monstrous|L6-0569]] creature. Or you are flying over your school, or a [[mischievous|L6-0560]] cat is reading your diary aloud to the whole class. Then you wake up. Dreams can be strange or frightening, and people have wondered about them for thousands of years. Many ancient peoples believed that dreams carried messages from the gods. Today, scientists study them in sleep labs.

Most vivid dreams happen during a stage of sleep called REM, short for "rapid eye movement." During REM sleep, the brain is almost as active as it is when we are awake, and our eyes move quickly under our closed [[eyelids|L6-0331]]. At the same time, most of the body's muscles become so relaxed that we can hardly move. This may keep us from acting out our dreams and running from that creature.

Why do we dream at all? One popular idea is that dreams help the brain sort through the [[miscellaneous|L6-0559]] memories of the day. In dreams, old memories [[mingle|L6-0557]] with new ones, which may explain why a childhood friend can suddenly appear in your present classroom. Another idea is that dreams let us practice dealing with danger in a safe place. A dream may [[mimic|L6-0556]] a real problem, such as being late for an exam, so that the mind can [[rehearse|L6-0744]] its response.

Dreams are closely tied to feelings. People who feel [[moody|L6-0570]] or stressed during the day often report more upsetting dreams, and after the loss of a loved one, dreams may be [[mournful|L6-0577]]. Some dreams are not upsetting but simply dull, repeating the [[monotony|L6-0568]] of daily life. The feeling a dream leaves behind can [[linger|L6-0510]] for hours after we wake.

Not everyone takes dreams seriously; some people have the [[mentality|L6-0552]] that they mean nothing at all. Yet dreams have served as a [[muse|L6-0579]] for many artists. The musician Paul McCartney has said that the melody of his famous song "Yesterday" came to him in a dream. So the next time you wake from a strange dream, write it down. It may mean more than you think.
zh: 你正被一隻怪物般的生物追趕。或者你正飛越學校上空，又或者一隻調皮的貓正對著全班大聲朗讀你的日記。然後你醒了。夢可能很奇怪，也可能很嚇人，數千年來人們一直對夢感到好奇。許多古代民族相信夢帶有眾神的訊息。如今，科學家則在睡眠實驗室裡研究夢。
大多數鮮明的夢發生在一個叫做 REM 的睡眠階段，也就是「快速動眼期」的縮寫。在 REM 睡眠期間，大腦幾乎和清醒時一樣活躍，眼球也在閉著的眼皮下快速轉動。同時，身體大部分的肌肉會放鬆到我們幾乎動不了。這或許能防止我們把夢境演出來，真的從那隻怪物面前逃跑。
我們到底為什麼會做夢？一種常見的說法是，夢幫助大腦整理白天各式各樣的記憶。在夢裡，舊記憶和新記憶交織在一起，這或許可以解釋為什麼童年的朋友會突然出現在你現在的教室裡。另一種說法是，夢讓我們在安全的地方練習應付危險。夢可能會模擬真實的問題，例如考試遲到，好讓大腦預先演練如何反應。
夢和情緒密切相關。白天心情起伏不定或壓力大的人，常說自己做了比較令人不安的夢；而在失去所愛的人之後，夢境可能充滿哀傷。有些夢並不令人不安，只是很無聊，重複著日常生活的單調。夢留下的感覺，可能在我們醒來後持續好幾個小時。
並不是每個人都認真看待夢；有些人抱持著夢毫無意義的心態。然而，夢曾經是許多藝術家的靈感來源。音樂家保羅・麥卡尼曾說，他的名曲〈Yesterday〉的旋律是在夢中出現的。所以下次你從奇怪的夢中醒來時，把它寫下來吧。它的意義也許比你想的還要多。

questions.stem: What happens to the body during REM sleep?
options: The eyes stay still while the brain rests.
The heart stops beating for a few seconds.
Most muscles relax so much that we can hardly move.
We often get out of bed and walk around.
questions.explain: 第二段說 REM 睡眠時，身體大部分的肌肉放鬆到幾乎動不了，故選 (C)。(A) 錯在此時眼球會快速轉動、大腦也很活躍。
questions.evidence: most of the body's muscles become so relaxed that we can hardly move

questions.stem: According to one idea in paragraph 3, how might dreams help us?
options: By letting us practice dealing with danger safely
By showing us what will happen in the future
By helping us forget everything from the day
By making us need less sleep
questions.explain: 第三段提到另一種說法：夢讓我們在安全的地方練習應付危險，例如模擬考試遲到，故選 (A)。(C) 錯在夢是「整理」記憶而非忘掉一切。
questions.evidence: dreams let us practice dealing with danger in a safe place

questions.stem: The word "mingle" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 舊記憶和新記憶 mingle，所以童年朋友會出現在現在的教室裡，可知是兩者「混合、交織」在一起，故選 (A) mix。(B) disappear（消失）無法解釋為何新舊人物會同時出現。
questions.evidence: old memories mingle with new ones

questions.stem: What does the writer most likely suggest in the last paragraph?
options: Dreams are messages from the gods.
Dreams may be worth paying attention to.
questions.explain: 最後一段舉麥卡尼在夢中得到旋律的例子，並建議讀者把奇怪的夢寫下來，可知作者認為夢值得留意，故選 (D)。(B) 是「有些人」的看法，作者並不同意。
questions.evidence: So the next time you wake from a strange dream, write it down.

vocab.stem: When the river flooded, hundreds of volunteers were quickly ______ to help families leave their homes.
vocab.explain: 河水氾濫時，數百名志工被迅速「動員」起來幫助家庭撤離，故選 mobilized。mowed（割草）、mingled（混合）、modernized（使現代化）都不能說明志工如何被召集。

vocab.stem: After losing five games in a row, the team's ______ was very low, so the coach planned a fun day at the beach.
vocab.explain: 連輸五場後，球隊的「士氣」很低落，所以教練安排去海邊玩一天打氣，故選 morale。monarch（君主）、mermaid（美人魚）、mound（土堆）都不能用「低落」來形容。

title: Three Keys to Changing Minds
paragraphs: Imagine you want your little brother to finish his [[oatmeal|L6-0600]] before school. You could [[nag|L6-0582]] him every morning, but nagging is [[notorious|L6-0592]] for making people want to resist even more. Persuasion, the art of changing someone's mind, works differently. More than 2,000 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle described three tools that good speakers use, and they still work today.

The first tool is trust. We are more likely to believe people who seem honest and who know what they are talking about. That is why a [[novice|L6-0594]] speaker often begins by explaining his or her experience, and why a doctor's advice about health carries more weight than a stranger's. If listeners do not find you [[credible|L6-0207]], even a [[notable|L6-0591]] fact may be ignored.

The second tool is emotion. Facts alone rarely move an audience; feelings do. Skilled speakers [[narrate|L6-0583]] a short story about one child or one family, because a single story stays in memory longer than a list of numbers. Listeners feel as if they are standing beside the [[narrator|L6-0584]]. A good story can [[evoke|L6-0316]] sympathy, hope, or even anger. However, emotion must be used honestly. Making people feel so guilty or afraid that they feel [[obliged|L6-0601]] to agree is not persuasion; it is pressure.

The third tool is reason. A clear case rests on evidence: examples, facts, and logical steps. The [[nucleus|L6-0595]] of a strong speech is usually one main claim supported by two or three solid reasons. Speakers who [[obsess|L6-0602]] over every small detail often lose their audience, while those who keep their point simple make it easy to follow.

Finally, good persuaders listen. They do not simply sit [[mute|L6-0581]], waiting for their turn to talk. They ask questions and admit when the other side has a fair point, which only [[enhances|L6-0305]] the trust others place in them. Changing a mind is not a common [[occurrence|L6-0604]], but with trust, feeling, and reason, it is possible. So the next time your brother refuses breakfast, try telling him a story instead of giving an order.
zh: 想像你希望弟弟上學前把燕麥粥吃完。你可以每天早上對他嘮叨，但出了名的是，嘮叨往往只會讓人更想反抗。說服——改變別人想法的藝術——的運作方式並不一樣。兩千多年前，希臘思想家亞里斯多德描述了優秀演說者會使用的三種工具，而它們到今天依然有效。
第一種工具是信任。我們比較容易相信看起來誠實、而且懂得自己在說什麼的人。這就是為什麼新手演講者常會先說明自己的經歷，也是為什麼醫生對健康的建議比陌生人的話更有分量。如果聽眾覺得你不可信，即使是值得注意的事實也可能被忽略。
第二種工具是情感。光有事實很少能打動聽眾；感受才能。熟練的演說者會講述一個關於某個孩子或某個家庭的小故事，因為單一的故事比一長串數字更容易留在記憶中。聽眾會覺得自己彷彿就站在講述者身旁。一個好故事能喚起同情、希望，甚至憤怒。不過，情感必須誠實地運用。讓人感到內疚或害怕，以致覺得自己不得不同意，那不是說服，而是施壓。
第三種工具是理性。清楚的論述建立在證據之上：例子、事實和合乎邏輯的步驟。一場有力演說的核心，通常是一個主要主張，再加上兩三個扎實的理由支撐。執著於每個小細節的演說者往往會失去聽眾，而把重點說得簡單的人，則讓人容易理解。
最後，好的說服者懂得傾聽。他們不會只是一言不發地坐著，等著輪到自己說話。他們會提出問題，並承認對方也有合理的論點，而這只會讓別人更信任他們。改變一個人的想法並不是常見的事，但有了信任、情感和理性，就有可能做到。所以下次弟弟不肯吃早餐時，試著講個故事給他聽，而不是下命令。

questions.stem: Why do skilled speakers often tell a story about one child or one family?
options: Stories are always shorter than facts.
A single story is remembered longer than a list of numbers.
Stories make the speaker look more experienced.
questions.explain: 第三段說熟練的演說者會講述關於一個孩子或一個家庭的故事，因為單一故事比一串數字更容易被記住，故選 (C)。(B) 與「感受才能打動聽眾」的說法相反。
questions.evidence: a single story stays in memory longer than a list of numbers

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT real persuasion?
options: Making people feel so guilty or afraid that they must agree
Supporting a claim with examples and facts
Admitting that the other side has a fair point
Explaining one's own experience to the audience
questions.explain: 第三段明確指出，讓人內疚或害怕到覺得不得不同意，不是說服而是施壓，故選 (A)。(B)、(C)、(D) 都是文中肯定的說服方法。
questions.evidence: Making people feel so guilty or afraid that they feel obliged to agree is not persuasion; it is pressure.

questions.stem: The word "nucleus" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 一場有力演說的 nucleus 通常是「一個主要主張」，再由兩三個理由支撐，可知 nucleus 指「核心」，故選 (B)。(C) 最弱的一點與「有力演說」的語意不合。
questions.evidence: The nucleus of a strong speech is usually one main claim supported by two or three solid reasons.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why nagging is the best way to deal with children
The life and works of Aristotle
How to win every argument by speaking louder
Trust, emotion, reason, and listening as ways to change minds
questions.explain: 文章以亞里斯多德的三種工具（信任、情感、理性）為主軸，最後再補充傾聽的重要，說明如何改變別人的想法，故選 (D)。(A) 與首段「嘮叨只會讓人更想反抗」相反。
questions.evidence: Aristotle described three tools that good speakers use, and they still work today

vocab.stem: Without her glasses, my ______ sister cannot read the words on the board from the back of the classroom.
vocab.explain: 沒戴眼鏡就看不清楚教室後方黑板上的字，表示姊姊「近視」，故選 nearsighted。offshore（離岸的）、notorious（惡名昭彰的）、mute（啞的）都無法說明為何看不清楚。

vocab.stem: The ship lost its way in the thick fog after its ______ system stopped working.
vocab.explain: 船在濃霧中迷失方向，是因為「導航」系統故障，故選 navigation。oath（誓言）、octopus（章魚）、nostril（鼻孔）都不是船上的系統。

title: City Debate Day: Motion and Rules
paragraphs:
NOTICE: Northfield City Debate Day
Date: Saturday, May 16, 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
Place: Hall B, Riverside Community Center, on the [[outskirts|L6-0632]] of town (a free bus leaves Northfield Station every 30 minutes)
This event is open to all high school students. It is a competition, but it is also a fun [[outing|L6-0624]] and a chance to meet students from other schools and [[broaden|L6-0103]] your [[outlook|L6-0626]].

THE MOTION
"This house would ban homework on weekends." Each school may send up to two teams of three speakers. Teams will learn at the [[outset|L6-0631]] of each round whether they will speak for or against the motion, so please prepare both sides.

RULES
1. Each speaker has four minutes. A bell will ring at three minutes as a warning. Speakers who go over the time limit will have points [[deducted|L6-0224]].
2. Respect your opponents. Personal attacks, shouting, and [[outrageous|L6-0629]] claims without evidence are not [[permissible|L6-0659]]. Judges will reward clear reasons, not loud voices.
3. Facts and numbers are welcome, but do not [[overdo|L6-0635]] them. A speech that is all numbers is hard to follow.
4. Keep team discussions quiet during a round; the other team should not be able to [[overhear|L6-0637]] your plans.
5. Audience members must remain seated and [[orderly|L6-0613]], with phones switched off. If Hall B is full, an [[overflow|L6-0636]] room next door will show the debate live on a large screen.

JUDGING
Three judges will score every round. A team that wins all three of its rounds will be named the [[outright|L6-0630]] winner. Cheering is allowed only between rounds. Even if one team's supporters [[outnumber|L6-0627]] the other's, this will have no effect on the result. Each round has a [[duration|L6-0287]] of about forty minutes, including time for the judges to give comments.

HOW TO SIGN UP
Please send your team list to the [[organizer|L6-0614]], Ms. Laura Chen, in Room 204 of Northfield High School by Friday, May 8. Lunch will be provided for all speakers.
zh:
公告：北原市辯論日
日期：5 月 16 日星期六，上午 9:00 至下午 4:00
地點：河畔社區中心 B 廳，位於市郊（北原車站每 30 分鐘有一班免費接駁車）
本活動開放所有高中生參加。這是一場比賽，但也是一次有趣的出遊，更是認識其他學校學生、開闊眼界的好機會。

辯題
「本院主張禁止週末出回家作業。」每校最多可派兩隊，每隊三名辯士。各隊會在每一輪開始時才知道自己要站在正方或反方，因此請兩方都做好準備。

規則
1. 每位辯士有四分鐘。第三分鐘時會響鈴提醒。超過時間限制的辯士將被扣分。
2. 請尊重對手。人身攻擊、大聲喊叫，以及沒有證據的荒唐說法都是不被允許的。評審會獎勵清楚的理由，而不是大的音量。
3. 歡迎使用事實和數字，但請勿過度。一篇全是數字的演說很難讓人聽懂。
4. 比賽進行中，隊內討論請保持小聲；不要讓對方隊伍聽到你們的計畫。
5. 觀眾必須坐在座位上並保持秩序，手機請關機。如果 B 廳坐滿，隔壁的備用場地會以大螢幕現場轉播比賽。

評分
每一輪由三位評審評分。三輪全勝的隊伍將成為無可爭議的冠軍。只有在兩輪之間才可以歡呼。即使某一隊的支持者人數比另一隊多，也不會影響比賽結果。每一輪時間約四十分鐘，包括評審講評的時間。

報名方式
請在 5 月 8 日星期五以前，將隊伍名單交給北原高中 204 教室的活動主辦人陳蘿拉老師。主辦單位會為所有辯士提供午餐。

questions.stem: When will teams find out which side of the motion they will speak for?
options: When they sign up for the event
At the start of each round
After the judges give their comments
questions.explain: 辯題段說各隊會在每一輪開始時才知道自己站在正方或反方，所以要兩方都準備，故選 (B)。(D) 評審講評是每輪結束時的事。
questions.evidence: Teams will learn at the outset of each round whether they will speak for or against the motion

questions.stem: What will happen if Hall B is full?
options: The event will be moved to another day.
People will have to stand at the back of the hall.
Some audience members can watch the debate in a room next door.
The organizer will send some people home.
questions.explain: 規則第 5 點說，如果 B 廳坐滿，隔壁的備用場地會以大螢幕現場轉播，故選 (C)。其他選項公告中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: If Hall B is full, an overflow room next door will show the debate live on a large screen.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most likely cause a speaker to lose points?
options: Using a few facts to support a point
Speaking in a calm and clear voice
Preparing to speak for both sides
Speaking for five minutes without stopping
questions.explain: 規則第 1 點說每位辯士只有四分鐘，超時會被扣分，所以講滿五分鐘最可能被扣分，故選 (D)。(A) 公告說歡迎使用事實，只是不要過度。
questions.evidence: Speakers who go over the time limit will have points deducted.

questions.stem: The word "outright" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 三輪全勝的隊伍會被稱為 outright winner，可知是「毫無疑問、完全的」冠軍，故選 (A)。(D) shared（共享的）與全勝獨得冠軍的情況相反。
questions.evidence: A team that wins all three of its rounds will be named the outright winner.

vocab.stem: We hung a small glass ______ in the window to catch the morning sunlight.
vocab.explain: 掛在窗邊、用來映照晨光的小玻璃物品是「裝飾品」，故選 ornament。ordeal（苦難）、ounce（盎司）、offspring（子女；後代）都不能用玻璃做成掛在窗上。

vocab.stem: The three hikers were lost in the mountains for two days. After such an ______, they were happy just to have a warm meal.
vocab.explain: 在山中迷路兩天是一場「痛苦的磨難」，所以他們光是吃到熱食就很開心，故選 ordeal（an ordeal）。outset（開端）、organizer（主辦人）、outlook（展望）都不能形容這段經歷。

title: Islands Against the Rising Sea
paragraphs: On many small islands in the Pacific and Indian Oceans, children grow up swimming, fishing, and learning to [[paddle|L6-0643]] a canoe almost as soon as they can walk. Collecting shells and [[pebbles|L6-0652]] along the beach is a favorite [[pastime|L6-0648]]. The sea gives these communities food, work, and joy. Yet it has also become their greatest [[peril|L6-0657]].

As the earth grows warmer, [[glaciers|L6-0380]] and other ice on land melt and flow into the ocean, and the water in the ocean expands as it heats up. Both cause sea levels to rise. For island nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati, and the Maldives, this is not a distant worry. Many of their islands are low [[coral|L6-0192]] islands, and much of their land lies only a meter or two above the sea, so even a small rise matters. During high tides and storms, salt water floods homes and roads. It also gets into the ground, spoiling drinking water and harming crops.

There is a painful [[paradox|L6-0645]] here. These small countries burn very little [[petroleum|L6-0664]] or coal, and they have produced only a tiny share of the gases that warm the planet. Yet they are among the first to suffer from the results.

Island communities have not given up. They [[persevere|L6-0660]] in many ways. They build walls along the [[coastline|L6-0159]], plant mangrove trees whose roots hold the soil in place, and move homes to higher ground. On islands where there is no higher ground, moving [[inland|L6-0453]] is not possible. The Maldives has built a new, higher island near its capital, and Kiribati has bought land in Fiji, partly so that it can grow food if its own fields fail. Many other plans are still [[pending|L6-0654]] because they cost more than small nations can pay.

The leaders of these countries have also been [[persistent|L6-0662]] in asking the rest of the world to act. Their message is simple: if nothing changes, whole nations could [[perish|L6-0658]] beneath the waves, and with them, languages, songs, and ways of life that have lasted for centuries.
zh: 在太平洋和印度洋的許多小島上，孩子們幾乎一學會走路，就跟著游泳、捕魚、學划獨木舟。沿著海灘撿貝殼和小石子是他們最喜歡的消遣。大海帶給這些社群食物、工作和歡樂，卻也成了他們最大的危險。
隨著地球越來越暖，冰河和陸地上的其他冰層融化、流入海洋，海水本身也會受熱膨脹。這兩者都會使海平面上升。對吐瓦魯、吉里巴斯和馬爾地夫等島國來說，這並不是遙遠的擔憂。他們的許多島嶼是低矮的珊瑚島，大部分土地只高出海面一兩公尺，所以即使海平面只上升一點點也影響重大。漲潮和暴風雨時，海水會淹進住家和道路，還會滲入地下，破壞飲用水並傷害農作物。
這裡存在著一個令人心痛的矛盾。這些小國很少燃燒石油或煤炭，排放的暖化氣體只占極小的比例，卻是最先承受後果的國家之一。
島嶼社群並沒有放棄。他們以許多方式堅持下去：沿著海岸線築牆、種植根部能固定土壤的紅樹林，並把住家遷往地勢較高的地方。在沒有高地的島上，往內陸遷移是不可能的。馬爾地夫在首都附近建造了一座地勢較高的新島；吉里巴斯則在斐濟買了土地，部分原因是萬一自己的農田無法耕作，還能在那裡種植糧食。還有許多計畫仍懸而未決，因為所需的費用超出這些小國的負擔能力。
這些國家的領袖也一直鍥而不捨地呼籲世界其他地方採取行動。他們的訊息很簡單：如果一切不改變，整個國家都可能沉沒於海浪之下，連同已經延續好幾個世紀的語言、歌謠和生活方式一起消失。

questions.stem: According to the passage, what are two causes of rising sea levels?
options: Melting ice on land and ocean water that expands as it warms
Earthquakes and volcanoes under the sea
More ships and fishing boats on the ocean
questions.explain: 第二段說陸地上的冰河與冰層融化流入海洋，海水也會受熱膨脹，兩者都讓海平面上升，故選 (B)。其他選項文中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: glaciers and other ice on land melt and flow into the ocean, and the water in the ocean expands as it heats up

questions.stem: Besides flooding homes and roads, how does salt water harm these islands?
options: It kills all the fish near the shore.
It makes the sand on the beaches too hot.
It breaks down the walls along the coast.
It spoils drinking water and harms crops.
questions.explain: 第二段說海水除了淹進住家和道路，還會滲入地下，破壞飲用水並傷害農作物，故選 (D)。(C) 海岸邊的牆是居民為了因應而建造的，文中沒說被海水破壞。
questions.evidence: It also gets into the ground, spoiling drinking water and harming crops.

questions.stem: What is the "paradox" mentioned in paragraph 3?
options: Countries that did little to cause the problem are among the first to suffer from it.
Island people love the sea but are also afraid of it.
Rich countries are building more and more islands.
Children learn to swim before they learn to walk.
questions.explain: 第三段說這些小國很少燃燒石油或煤炭、排放極少，卻是最先受害的國家，這就是文中的「矛盾」，故選 (A)。(D) 第一段只說孩子一學會走路就學划船。
questions.evidence: Yet they are among the first to suffer from the results.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about islands that have no higher ground?
options: Their people will never need to move.
They are safe from storms and high tides.
They may need solutions such as building new land or finding land elsewhere.
They produce a large amount of petroleum.
questions.explain: 第四段說沒有高地的島無法往內陸遷移，接著舉馬爾地夫建新島、吉里巴斯在斐濟買地的例子，可推知它們需要另找土地或造地，故選 (C)。(D) 與第三段「很少燃燒石油」的敘述無關且不合。
questions.evidence: On islands where there is no higher ground, moving inland is not possible.

vocab.stem: Please don't ______ at your birthday presents before the party starts!
vocab.explain: 派對開始前別「偷看」生日禮物，peek at 是固定用法，故選 peek。perish（死亡）、paddle（划槳）、overwork（過度工作）都不能接 at your presents。

vocab.stem: The male ______ opened its beautiful blue and green tail feathers to attract attention.
vocab.explain: 會展開藍綠色美麗尾羽吸引注意的雄性動物是「孔雀」，故選 peacock。paperback（平裝書）、pharmacist（藥劑師）、peninsula（半島）都沒有羽毛。

title: Treasures That Belong to Everyone
paragraphs: In the 1960s, Egypt began building a huge dam on the Nile River. The lake behind it would cover the temples of Abu Simbel, which had been cut into a cliff more than 3,000 years earlier. Instead of letting these [[majestic|L6-0538]] buildings disappear, many countries helped pay for an amazing rescue. Engineers cut the temples into large blocks, moved them to higher ground, and put them back together with great [[precision|L6-0688]].

This rescue set an important [[precedent|L6-0687]]. It showed that some places are so valuable that protecting them is the duty of all humanity, not only of the country where they stand. In 1972, UNESCO, a United Nations agency, adopted an agreement to protect such places, and the first World Heritage Sites were named in 1978.

Today the list includes more than a thousand sites, from forests and mountains to [[prehistoric|L6-0690]] monuments such as Stonehenge in England, whose huge stones were raised by people who [[preceded|L6-0686]] the Romans in Britain by thousands of years. It also includes [[medieval|L6-0548]] towns, ancient temples, and even routes. For over a thousand years, [[pilgrims|L6-0669]] have walked the long roads across Europe to the city of Santiago de Compostela in Spain, and parts of these roads are now protected as well.

Being on the list brings [[prestige|L6-0693]] and visitors, but it also brings problems. Large crowds can wear down old floors and walls, and busy streets attract [[pickpockets|L6-0668]]. In some popular cities, people who live near famous sites complain that crowds make it hard even to walk to the [[pharmacy|L6-0666]] or the market. Money from visitors can pay for [[restoration|L6-0761]] work, but too many visitors can create the damage that needs repairing.

Visitors can help by following local rules, staying on paths, and taking only photos. As you stand before a place that has survived for centuries, take a moment to [[ponder|L6-0678]] the people who built it. Our [[predecessors|L6-0689]] left these treasures to us, and it is now our turn to pass them on to the generations that will follow.
zh: 1960 年代，埃及開始在尼羅河上興建一座巨大的水壩。水壩後方形成的湖將會淹沒阿布辛貝神殿——這座神殿早在三千多年前就鑿刻在懸崖上。許多國家沒有讓這些雄偉的建築就此消失，而是幫忙出資進行了一場驚人的搶救行動。工程師把神殿切割成大石塊，搬到地勢較高的地方，再以極高的精準度重新組合起來。
這次搶救行動立下了一個重要的先例。它顯示有些地方珍貴到保護它們是全人類的責任，而不只是它們所在國家的責任。1972 年，聯合國的機構「聯合國教科文組織」通過了一項保護這類地方的協議，第一批世界遺產則在 1978 年公布。
如今，這份名單包含一千多處遺產，從森林、山岳，到史前時代的古蹟，例如英格蘭的巨石陣——那些巨大的石頭，是由比羅馬人早數千年來到不列顛的人們立起來的。名單中也有中世紀的城鎮、古老的神殿，甚至還有路線。一千多年來，朝聖者走過橫越歐洲的漫漫長路，前往西班牙的聖地牙哥－德孔波斯特拉，如今這些道路有部分也受到保護。
被列入名單會帶來聲望和遊客，但也帶來問題。大批人潮可能磨損古老的地板和牆面，熱鬧的街道也會吸引扒手。在一些熱門城市，住在知名遺產附近的居民抱怨，人潮多到連走去藥局或市場都很困難。遊客帶來的收入可以支付修復工程，但過多的遊客也可能造成需要修復的損害。
遊客可以透過遵守當地規定、走在步道上、只帶走照片來盡一份力。當你站在一個留存了好幾個世紀的地方面前，花點時間思考建造它的人們吧。我們的前人把這些寶藏留給了我們，現在輪到我們把它們傳給後代。

questions.stem: Why did the temples of Abu Simbel need to be rescued?
options: They had been damaged by an earthquake.
Visitors had worn down their walls.
They had been sold to another country.
A lake created by a new dam would cover them.
questions.explain: 第一段說埃及在尼羅河上建水壩，水壩後方形成的湖會淹沒阿布辛貝神殿，故選 (D)。(B) 遊客磨損牆面是第四段談的一般問題。
questions.evidence: The lake behind it would cover the temples of Abu Simbel

questions.stem: The word "precedent" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ______.
options: an example that guides later actions
a mistake that should be avoided
a gift from one country to another
questions.explain: 這次搶救行動「顯示」某些地方是全人類的責任，之後才有 1972 年的協議與世界遺產名單，可知 precedent 指可供日後依循的「先例」，故選 (A)。(B) 搶救是成功的，並非該避免的錯誤。
questions.evidence: This rescue set an important precedent.

questions.stem: Which problem caused by large numbers of visitors is mentioned?
options: Hotel prices go up in the countryside.
Visitors take stones home from the sites.
Local people find it hard to do simple daily tasks.
The sites must close every night.
questions.explain: 第四段說住在知名遺產附近的居民抱怨，人潮多到連走去藥局或市場都很困難，故選 (C)。其他選項文中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: crowds make it hard even to walk to the pharmacy or the market

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Egypt has more World Heritage Sites than any other country.
Everyone should walk the old roads to Spain.
People should stop traveling to famous places.
World Heritage Sites belong to all people, who share the duty to protect them.
questions.explain: 文章從阿布辛貝的搶救談起，說明世界遺產是全人類的責任，再談觀光帶來的問題與遊客能做的事，最後強調要把寶藏傳給後代，故選 (D)。(C) 文章只建議遊客守規矩，並未要人停止旅行。
questions.evidence: protecting them is the duty of all humanity

vocab.stem: The hotel ______ helped us carry our heavy bags up to our room.
vocab.explain: 在飯店幫忙把沉重行李搬上樓的人是「行李員」，故選 porter。plague（瘟疫）、premiere（首映）、pimple（青春痘）都不會搬行李。

vocab.stem: Sitting with good ______, with your back straight and shoulders relaxed, can help prevent back pain.
vocab.explain: 背打直、肩膀放鬆，是良好的「坐姿」，可以預防背痛，故選 posture。pony（小馬）、pharmacy（藥局）、poultry（家禽）都不能用來描述坐的方式。

title: When the Wolves Came Home
paragraphs: For centuries, wolves have had a [[notorious|L6-0592]] reputation. In fairy tales they appear as [[monstrous|L6-0569]] enemies, and farmers have long feared for their sheep and cattle. In the United States, this fear led to years of hunting, and by the 1920s the last wolf packs in Yellowstone National Park had disappeared. At the time, few people [[pondered|L6-0678]] what the park had lost.

Without wolves, elk had no major natural enemy. Their numbers grew, and large herds stayed close to rivers and streams, [[grazing|L6-0392]] on young willow trees before the trees could grow tall. Over the following decades, scientists noticed that many river banks were becoming bare. Some began to argue that the missing predator was the key to the problem.

In 1995 and 1996, after years of debate, wildlife officials brought gray wolves from Canada and released them in the park. There was little [[precedent|L6-0687]] for such a plan, and some local farmers reacted with [[outrage|L6-0628]], fearing for their animals. The wolves, however, did well. They formed packs, raised [[offspring|L6-0608]], and spread across the area, and the project quickly gained [[momentum|L6-0565]].

What happened next has become one of the most [[notable|L6-0591]] stories in modern ecology. With wolves around, elk moved more often and spent less time in open river valleys. In some places, willows grew back, and beavers returned to build dams, creating ponds where fish and birds could [[flourish|L6-0352]]. Supporters point out a [[paradox|L6-0645]]: a hunter of other animals helped bring a whole valley back to life.

Yet many scientists remain careful. They argue that the story has been made too simple. Changes in weather, other predators such as bears, and human hunting outside the park also played a role, and these effects [[overlap|L6-0638]] in ways that are hard to separate. The [[outlook|L6-0626]] for the wolves themselves is not certain, either, because those that wander beyond the park's borders face [[peril|L6-0657]]. Still, thanks to the [[persistent|L6-0662]] work of researchers, Yellowstone has become a model for the [[restoration|L6-0761]] of wild places around the world. Its lesson is clear: removing one animal from nature can change far more than we expect.
zh: 好幾個世紀以來，狼的名聲一直很差。在童話故事裡，牠們以怪物般的反派形象出現，農民也長久以來擔心自家的羊和牛。在美國，這種恐懼導致了多年的獵捕，到了 1920 年代，黃石國家公園裡最後的狼群也消失了。當時，很少有人思考這座公園失去了什麼。
沒有了狼，麋鹿就沒有主要的天敵。牠們的數量增加，大群麋鹿聚集在河流與溪流附近，在柳樹長高之前就把幼樹吃掉。在接下來的幾十年裡，科學家注意到許多河岸變得光禿禿的。有些人開始主張，消失的掠食者正是問題的關鍵。
經過多年的爭論，野生動物官員在 1995 和 1996 年從加拿大引進灰狼，並將牠們野放到公園裡。這樣的計畫幾乎沒有先例可循，一些當地農民憤怒不已，擔心自己的牲畜。不過，這些狼適應得很好。牠們組成狼群、繁衍後代，並擴散到整個地區，這項計畫也迅速取得進展。
接下來發生的事，成了現代生態學中最著名的故事之一。有狼出沒之後，麋鹿移動得更頻繁，在開闊的河谷裡停留的時間也變少了。在某些地方，柳樹重新長了回來，河狸也回來築壩，形成讓魚類和鳥類得以繁盛的池塘。支持者指出其中的矛盾：一種獵捕其他動物的動物，竟幫助整座山谷恢復了生機。
然而，許多科學家仍然保持謹慎。他們認為這個故事被過度簡化了。天氣的變化、熊等其他掠食者，以及公園外人類的狩獵，也都發揮了作用，而這些影響彼此重疊，很難區分開來。狼本身的前景也不確定，因為走出公園邊界的狼會面臨危險。儘管如此，多虧研究人員鍥而不捨的努力，黃石公園已成為世界各地恢復野生環境的典範。它的啟示很清楚：從大自然中移除一種動物，所造成的改變可能遠超乎我們的預期。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why farmers have always hated wolves
How beavers build dams and ponds
How wolves returned to Yellowstone and what scientists think about their effects
Fairy tales in which wolves are the villains
questions.explain: 文章先說明狼如何從黃石公園消失，再談 1995、1996 年重新引進狼之後生態的變化，最後介紹科學家對這些影響的不同看法，故選 (C)。(D) 童話只是第一段的引子。
questions.evidence: What happened next has become one of the most notable stories in modern ecology.

questions.stem: What happened to many river banks while there were no wolves in the park?
options: They were covered with tall willow trees.
They became bare because elk ate the young trees.
They were flooded by beaver dams.
Bears moved in and dug them up.
questions.explain: 第二段說沒有狼之後麋鹿大增，聚在河邊把柳樹幼苗吃掉，科學家注意到許多河岸變得光禿禿，故選 (B)。(A)、(C) 是狼回來之後才出現的情況。
questions.evidence: many river banks were becoming bare

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the last paragraph?
options: All scientists agree that wolves alone saved the park.
Wolves no longer live in Yellowstone.
Wolves were probably only one of several causes of the changes.
Scientists plan to remove the wolves again.
questions.explain: 最後一段說天氣、熊等其他掠食者和人類狩獵也發揮了作用，各種影響彼此重疊、難以區分，可推知狼可能只是造成變化的原因之一，故選 (C)。(A) 與「許多科學家保持謹慎」相反。
questions.evidence: these effects overlap in ways that are hard to separate

questions.stem: The "paradox" in paragraph 4 refers to the fact that ______.
options: wolves eat elk but stay away from valleys
a hunter of other animals helped a valley come back to life
beavers and fish live in the same ponds
questions.explain: 第四段冒號後說明了這個矛盾：一種獵捕其他動物的動物，竟幫助整座山谷恢復生機，故選 (B)。「掠食者」與「帶來生機」看似相反，正是 paradox（矛盾）的意思。
questions.evidence: a hunter of other animals helped bring a whole valley back to life

vocab.stem: The young ______ was nervous before her first concert, but she played every note perfectly.
vocab.explain: 在第一場音樂會前緊張、卻把每個音符都彈得完美的人是「鋼琴家」，故選 pianist。plow（犁）、pony（小馬）、pickpocket（扒手）都不會開音樂會。

vocab.stem: The film's ______ was held in Taipei, and the actors walked on the red carpet before the first showing.
vocab.explain: 電影在台北舉行、演員走紅毯、接著第一次放映，這是電影的「首映」，故選 premiere。plague（瘟疫）、poultry（家禽）、pneumonia（肺炎）都與走紅毯無關。

title: From Bitter Drink to Sweet Bar
paragraphs: Long before chocolate came in bars and boxes, it was a [[beverage|L6-0083]], and not a sweet one. In ancient Central America, the Maya and later the Aztecs roasted and ground cacao beans, mixed them with water and spices such as [[chili|L6-0145]], and poured the drink from one cup to another to create a thick foam. The Aztecs valued the beans so highly that they even used them as money. To them, a handful of cacao was almost [[priceless|L6-0696]].

Spanish explorers brought cacao to Europe in the 1500s. At first, many Europeans found the bitter drink strange. Once it was mixed with sugar and [[vanilla|L6-0956]], however, it became a fashion among the rich. In royal courts, a cup of hot chocolate was a sign of wealth and good taste, and over time the drink spread from the capitals to [[provincial|L6-0708]] towns. Some people even bought it at the [[pharmacy|L6-0666]], believing that it was good for their health.

A big change came in 1828, when a Dutch [[chemist|L6-0143]] named Coenraad van Houten developed a machine that pressed much of the fat out of cacao. What remained could be made into a fine powder that mixed easily with water. This invention helped [[propel|L6-0702]] chocolate from a luxury toward a food that ordinary people could afford. In 1847, a British company mixed cocoa powder, sugar, and the fat from the beans to make a solid bar that became the [[prototype|L6-0706]] of the chocolate bars we eat today. In the 1870s, Swiss makers learned to add milk, creating smooth milk chocolate.

As factories grew, companies began to [[publicize|L6-0713]] their products with colorful posters and promises of [[purity|L6-0717]]. Shops handed out free samples so that [[prospective|L6-0705]] customers could get a sweet [[preview|L6-0695]] before buying. Writers praised chocolate in poems and [[prose|L6-0703]], and the warm smell that [[radiated|L6-0721]] from chocolate shops drew people in from the street.

From a bitter drink for kings to a sweet that costs only a few coins, chocolate has traveled a long way. The next time a piece melts on your tongue, remember that you are tasting thousands of years of history.
zh: 早在巧克力做成一條條、一盒盒之前，它是一種飲料，而且不是甜的。在古代的中美洲，馬雅人和後來的阿茲特克人會把可可豆烘烤、磨碎，加入水和辣椒等香料，再把飲料從一個杯子倒到另一個杯子，打出濃厚的泡沫。阿茲特克人非常珍視可可豆，甚至拿它當錢使用。對他們來說，一把可可豆幾乎是無價之寶。
西班牙探險家在 1500 年代把可可帶到歐洲。起初，許多歐洲人覺得這種苦澀的飲料很奇怪。然而一加入糖和香草後，它就成了有錢人之間的時尚。在皇家宮廷裡，一杯熱巧克力是財富與品味的象徵；隨著時間過去，這種飲料從各國首都傳到了地方城鎮。有些人甚至會到藥房購買巧克力，相信它對健康有益。
一大轉變出現在 1828 年。當時一位名叫柯恩拉德・范豪頓的荷蘭化學家，研發出一種能把可可中大部分油脂壓出來的機器。剩下的部分可以做成容易溶於水的細緻粉末。這項發明推動巧克力從奢侈品，逐漸變成一般人買得起的食物。1847 年，一家英國公司把可可粉、糖和可可豆的油脂混合在一起，做出一塊固體的巧克力，成為我們今天所吃巧克力片的原型。1870 年代，瑞士的製造商學會加入牛奶，做出了滑順的牛奶巧克力。
隨著工廠規模擴大，公司開始用色彩繽紛的海報宣傳產品，並保證產品純正。商店發放免費試吃品，讓潛在顧客在購買前先甜甜地嘗鮮。作家們在詩歌與散文中讚美巧克力，而巧克力店散發出的溫暖香氣，也把街上的行人吸引進門。
從獻給君王的苦澀飲料，到只要幾枚硬幣就買得到的甜食，巧克力走過了漫長的路。下一次當一塊巧克力在你舌尖融化時，記得你嘗到的是數千年的歷史。

questions.stem: How was chocolate first enjoyed in ancient Central America?
options: As a bitter drink mixed with spices
As a medicine sold in shops
As a cake made for kings
questions.explain: 第一段說馬雅人和阿茲特克人把可可豆磨碎，加入水和辣椒等香料做成飲料，而且「不是甜的」，故選 (B)。(C) 在藥房購買是巧克力傳入歐洲之後的事。
questions.evidence: mixed them with water and spices such as chili

questions.stem: What did Coenraad van Houten's machine do?
options: It turned chocolate into solid bars.
It pressed fat out of cacao, leaving a fine powder.
It helped farmers grow cacao in Europe.
questions.explain: 第三段說范豪頓研發的機器能把可可中大部分油脂壓出來，剩下的部分可以做成細緻粉末，故選 (C)。(A) 加牛奶是 1870 年代瑞士製造商的成就，(B) 做成固體巧克力是 1847 年一家英國公司。
questions.evidence: developed a machine that pressed much of the fat out of cacao

questions.stem: The word "provincial" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ______.
options: far from the capital or big cities
questions.explain: 熱巧克力「從首都傳到 provincial 城鎮」，與首都相對，可知是「首都以外的、地方上的」，故選 (A)。(B) 皇家是前一句的宮廷，不是這些城鎮的特色。
questions.evidence: the drink spread from the capitals to provincial towns

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the passage?
options: Chocolate has always been a cheap food.
Europeans loved the bitter drink from the very start.
The Aztecs added milk to their chocolate drinks.
New inventions helped make chocolate affordable for ordinary people.
questions.explain: 第三段說范豪頓的發明推動巧克力從奢侈品變成一般人買得起的食物，之後又有固體巧克力和牛奶巧克力，故選 (D)。(B) 文中說歐洲人起初覺得這種苦飲料很奇怪。
questions.evidence: This invention helped propel chocolate from a luxury toward a food that ordinary people could afford.

vocab.stem: The train always leaves exactly on time, so please be ______; it will not wait for anyone.
vocab.explain: 火車一定準時開、不等任何人，所以要「準時的」，故選 punctual。psychic（通靈的）、radiant（容光煥發的）、provisional（暫時的）都與趕上火車無關。

vocab.stem: There is a strict ______ on smoking inside all school buildings.
vocab.explain: 學校建築內抽菸受到嚴格的「禁止」，a prohibition on sth. 是常見用法，故選 prohibition。procession（遊行隊伍）、psychiatry（精神醫學）、qualification（資格）都不能接 on smoking 表示禁令。

title: Think Before the World Sees It
paragraphs: Sixteen-year-old Mia posted a photo of herself in her new school uniform. A few hours later, a classmate pointed out that the picture showed the name of her school, a street sign near her home, and the time she left each morning. The [[realization|L6-0728]] made her stomach drop. She had shared far more than she had meant to.

Stories like Mia's are common. Most teenagers are not [[reckless|L6-0730]]; they simply do not [[reckon|L6-0731]] with how much a single post can reveal. Photos may carry hidden location data, and some apps can show where you are to anyone within a certain [[radius|L6-0724]]. Once information is online, it can be copied and [[relayed|L6-0747]] to strangers in seconds, and taking down the original does not get rid of the copies. Even old posts may stay online for years, like [[relics|L6-0751]] of a past you have left behind.

Companies also collect information in [[relentless|L6-0748]] ways. Free games and websites often record what you click, how long you watch, and what you buy, and then use that information to show you ads. Because we are so [[reliant|L6-0750]] on our phones for school, friends, and [[recreational|L6-0733]] activities, it is hard to avoid this completely. A [[hacker|L6-0397]] who breaks into an account with a weak password can also learn a great deal.

A few simple habits can help. First, check the privacy settings on every account, and make your posts visible only to people you know. Second, turn off location sharing unless you really need it. Third, before you post, pause and be [[reflective|L6-0739]]: Would I be comfortable if a teacher, a future employer, or a stranger saw this? Being [[discreet|L6-0260]] about your address, your school, and your daily plans is not the same as hiding. Think of every post as a public [[disclosure|L6-0258]].

Some teens [[resent|L6-0757]] such warnings and feel that adults are trying to control them. That feeling makes sense, but privacy is not about fear; it is about choice. With a little care, it is possible to [[reconcile|L6-0732]] the fun of sharing with the need to stay safe.
zh: 十六歲的蜜雅貼了一張自己穿新制服的照片。幾個小時後，一位同學指出，照片裡看得到她學校的名字、她家附近的路牌，以及她每天早上出門的時間。意識到這一點讓她的心一沉。她分享的東西，遠比她原本想的多得多。
像蜜雅這樣的事很常見。大多數青少年並不魯莽，他們只是沒有考慮到一則貼文能透露多少資訊。照片可能帶有隱藏的位置資料，有些應用程式也會把你的位置顯示給一定半徑範圍內的任何人。資訊一旦上網，幾秒鐘內就能被複製、轉傳給陌生人，而撤下原始貼文並不能清除那些副本。就連舊貼文也可能在網路上留存好幾年，就像你早已告別的過去所留下的遺跡。
公司也以無孔不入的方式蒐集資訊。免費的遊戲和網站常會記錄你點了什麼、看了多久、買了什麼，再利用這些資訊向你推送廣告。因為我們在課業、交友和休閒活動上都如此依賴手機，要完全避免這種情況很難。駭客如果入侵一個密碼太簡單的帳號，也能知道很多事情。
有幾個簡單的習慣可以幫上忙。第一，檢查每個帳號的隱私設定，讓貼文只有你認識的人看得到。第二，除非真的需要，否則關閉位置分享。第三，發文前先停下來想一想：如果老師、未來的雇主或陌生人看到這則貼文，我會覺得自在嗎？對自己的地址、學校和每天的行程保持謹慎，並不等於躲躲藏藏。把每一則貼文都當作一次公開的揭露吧。
有些青少年對這類提醒感到不滿，覺得大人想要控制他們。這種感受可以理解，但隱私無關恐懼，而是關於選擇。只要多一點用心，分享的樂趣和保護自身安全的需要，是可以兼顧的。

questions.stem: What did Mia's photo accidentally show?
options: Her school's name, a street sign near her home, and when she left each morning
Her phone number and her password
Her grades from the last school year
questions.explain: 第一段說同學指出照片裡看得到她學校的名字、家附近的路牌，以及她每天早上出門的時間，故選 (A)。其他選項文中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: the picture showed the name of her school, a street sign near her home, and the time she left each morning

questions.stem: Why is taking down a post not always enough?
options: The phone keeps a second copy of every photo.
Teachers are always able to see deleted posts.
Copies may already have been passed on to other people.
Hackers will post it again under a new name.
questions.explain: 第二段說資訊一旦上網，幾秒內就可能被複製、轉傳給陌生人，撤下原始貼文並不能清除那些副本，故選 (C)。(D) 文中提到駭客，但沒說他們會重新貼文。
questions.evidence: taking down the original does not get rid of the copies

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, why are old posts compared to "relics"?
options: They are worth a lot of money.
They remain from the past even after we have changed.
They are kept safely in museums.
questions.explain: 文中說舊貼文可能在網路上留存好幾年，就像「你早已告別的過去」留下的 relics（遺跡），重點在於人已經改變、東西卻還留著，故選 (B)。(D) 與「留存好幾年」相反。
questions.evidence: Even old posts may stay online for years, like relics of a past you have left behind.

questions.stem: What is the writer's main point?
options: Teenagers should stop using their phones.
Adults should take control of teenagers' accounts.
Companies never collect information about teenagers.
With careful habits, teens can enjoy sharing while protecting their privacy.
questions.explain: 作者說明貼文可能洩漏的資訊，提出幾個簡單習慣，最後強調隱私關乎選擇，分享的樂趣和安全可以兼顧，故選 (D)。(A)、(B) 都比作者的建議極端得多，(C) 與第三段相反。
questions.evidence: it is possible to reconcile the fun of sharing with the need to stay safe

vocab.stem: The ______ blew his whistle and showed the player a yellow card.
vocab.explain: 會吹哨並對球員出示黃牌的人是「裁判」，故選 referee。radish（蘿蔔）、referendum（公民投票）、reptile（爬蟲類）都不會吹哨子。

vocab.stem: The smell of fresh rain is ______ of the summers I spent on my grandmother's farm.
vocab.explain: 雨後清新的氣味「令人想起」在外婆農場度過的夏天，be reminiscent of 是固定用法，故選 reminiscent。reckless（魯莽的）、radioactive（放射性的）、recreational（休閒的）都不能接 of 表示「使人想起」。

title: Waking a Sleeping Language
paragraphs: When the last speaker of a language dies, a whole way of seeing the world can disappear with her. Linguists warn that many of the world's languages may not survive this century. In the past, children in many places were punished for speaking their home languages at school, and some grew up to [[scorn|L6-0787]] the words of their own grandparents as old-fashioned. Once parents stop passing a language on to their children, it can fade within a few generations, and whole communities [[mourn|L6-0576]] the loss.

Yet a fading language is not always lost forever. The most famous [[revival|L6-0767]] is that of Hebrew. For nearly two thousand years, it was used mainly for prayer and study rather than for daily conversation. In the late 1800s, Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and others set out to [[revive|L6-0768]] it as a spoken language. They created new words for modern objects and insisted on speaking Hebrew at home. Today millions of people speak it every day.

In Hawaii, by the early 1980s, very few children could speak Hawaiian. In 1984, a group of parents and teachers opened a nursery school where young children heard and spoke only Hawaiian all day. To prepare lessons, teachers had to [[retrieve|L6-0765]] old songs, stories, and recordings from [[archives|L6-0055]] and from elderly speakers, [[salvaging|L6-0783]] what they could before it was too late. Over the years, the project grew into a [[robust|L6-0775]] system of schools, from nursery school to high school.

Similar work is being done in Taiwan, where Indigenous peoples, from fishing villages on the coast to [[rugged|L6-0780]] mountain towns, are working to keep their [[respective|L6-0760]] languages alive through classes, dictionaries, radio programs, and online videos. Such work demands [[rigorous|L6-0771]] practice, since learners must master new sounds, grammar, and stories. For many young learners, however, discovering their grandparents' words has been a [[revelation|L6-0766]]. A language, they find, is not [[rubbish|L6-0779]] to be thrown away but a living [[relic|L6-0751]] of their history. Every new speaker starts a [[ripple|L6-0772]] that may one day reach a whole community, and each word saved makes the whole [[endeavor|L6-0302]] worthwhile.
zh: 當一種語言的最後一位使用者離世，一整套看世界的方式也可能隨她一起消失。語言學家警告，世界上許多語言可能撐不過這個世紀。過去在許多地方，孩子在學校說自己的母語會被處罰，有些人長大後甚至瞧不起祖父母說的話，認為那很老土。一旦父母不再把語言傳給孩子，它可能在幾代之內就消失，整個族群都會為這樣的失去而哀悼。
然而，一種逐漸消失的語言不一定就此永遠失傳。最著名的語言復興例子是希伯來語。將近兩千年來，它主要用於祈禱和研讀經典，而不是日常對話。十九世紀末，艾利澤・本－耶胡達等人決心讓它重新成為口說語言。他們為現代事物創造新詞，並堅持在家裡說希伯來語。如今，數百萬人每天都在使用它。
在夏威夷，到了 1980 年代初期，會說夏威夷語的孩子已經非常少。1984 年，一群家長和老師開辦了一所幼兒園，讓孩子整天只聽、只說夏威夷語。為了準備課程，老師們必須從檔案資料和年長的使用者那裡找回古老的歌曲、故事和錄音，趁還來得及的時候盡量搶救。多年來，這項計畫發展成一套穩固的學校體系，從幼兒園一路到高中。

台灣也在進行類似的努力。從海邊的漁村到崎嶇的山中部落，各原住民族正透過課程、字典、廣播節目和網路影片，努力讓各自的語言延續下去。這樣的工作需要嚴格紮實的練習，因為學習者必須熟練新的發音、文法和故事。不過，對許多年輕學習者來說，發現祖父母的語言就像是一種啟示。他們發現，語言不是該丟掉的垃圾，而是承載自己歷史、依然活著的遺產。每一位新的使用者都會激起一圈漣漪，有一天可能擴及整個族群；而每多保存一個詞，這份努力就更加值得。

questions.stem: What did Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and others do in the late 1800s?
options: They recorded the last people who spoke Hebrew.
They worked to bring Hebrew back as a spoken language.
They translated old prayers into modern languages.
They opened the first Hebrew-only nursery school.
questions.explain: 第二段說十九世紀末，本－耶胡達等人決心讓希伯來語重新成為口說語言，並為現代事物創造新詞，故選 (B)。(D) 全語言幼兒園是第三段夏威夷的例子。
questions.evidence: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and others set out to revive it as a spoken language

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, where did teachers in Hawaii find materials for their lessons?
options: In old archives and from elderly speakers
In songs written by their students
questions.explain: 第三段說老師們必須從檔案資料和年長的使用者那裡找回歌曲、故事和錄音，故選 (A)。其他選項文中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: recordings from archives and from elderly speakers

questions.stem: The word "robust" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 這項計畫從一所幼兒園「發展成」一路到高中的學校體系，可知 robust 指「穩固、健全的」，故選 (C)。(A) 容易損壞的意思正好相反。
questions.evidence: the project grew into a robust system of schools

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Young people today no longer respect old languages.
Hebrew is the only language that has ever been revived.
Taiwan's Indigenous languages are easier to learn than Hawaiian.
Fading languages can be brought back through hard work and community effort.
questions.explain: 文章先談語言消失的危機，再以希伯來語、夏威夷語和台灣原住民族語為例，說明語言可以靠努力復興，故選 (D)。(B) 文中舉了不只一個復興的例子。
questions.evidence: Yet a fading language is not always lost forever.

vocab.stem: After the flood, volunteers worked for days to ______ family photos and other treasures from the damaged houses.
vocab.explain: 志工在淹水後花好幾天從受損的房屋中「搶救」家庭照片等珍貴物品，故選 salvage。salute（敬禮）、scorn（輕視）、retort（反駁）都不能接「照片」當受詞表示搶救。

vocab.stem: The trail climbs through ______ mountains with sharp rocks and steep cliffs, so only experienced hikers should try it.
vocab.explain: 山路滿是尖石和陡峭懸崖，可知山勢「崎嶇的」，故選 rugged。respective（各自的）、robust（強健的）、ruthless（無情的）都不能形容山的地形。

title: Two Lenses and a Paper Tube
paragraphs: Ting was [[scrolling|L6-0790]] through videos on her phone when her grandfather called her into the garage. In the corner sat a [[shabby|L6-0802]] [[cardboard|L6-0120]] box covered in dust. Inside were two glass lenses, a long paper tube, and a page of instructions he had kept for forty years. "When I was your age, I wanted to build a telescope," he said. "I never finished it. Shall we try?" Ting was [[skeptical|L6-0815]]. Could old glass and a paper tube really show her anything?

They began that weekend. Ting [[skimmed|L6-0816]] the instructions, eager to start, but Grandpa read every line slowly and held each lens up to the light for careful [[scrutiny|L6-0791]]. He pointed to a [[screwdriver|L6-0789]] on the shelf, and Ting tightened the tiny screws that held the lenses in place. Their first [[setback|L6-0801]] came quickly. When they aimed the tube at the moon, everything looked blurry. The lenses, Grandpa explained, were the wrong distance apart, so each evening they moved them a little and tested again.

After a week, Ting began to lose patience. "Why don't we just buy a telescope online?" she asked. Grandpa smiled. "We could. But a store-bought one would hide how it works. I love the [[simplicity|L6-0812]] of two lenses and a tube. Every [[shortcoming|L6-0805]] we find teaches us something." Then he admitted that it had been [[shortsighted|L6-0806]] of him to give up as a boy just because his first try had failed.

One clear night in October, they set the telescope up at Grandpa's bedroom window. Grandpa [[shuffled|L6-0810]] in slowly in his slippers, and Ting pushed open the old wooden [[shutters|L6-0811]]. She aimed the tube at the moon, adjusted it once more, and [[shrieked|L6-0808]] with joy. The [[craters|L6-0206]] stood out sharp and clear, as if someone had [[magnified|L6-0535]] a photograph. Beside her, Grandpa looked [[serene|L6-0796]], as though a forty-year-old wish had quietly come true.
Later, Ting realized they had built more than a telescope. By [[simplifying|L6-0813]] one big problem into many small steps, they had also built patience.
zh: 婷正在用手機滑影片，爺爺把她叫進車庫。角落放著一個積滿灰塵、破舊的紙箱。裡面有兩片玻璃鏡片、一根長長的紙筒，還有一張他保存了四十年的說明書。「我在妳這個年紀的時候，很想做一架望遠鏡，」他說，「可是一直沒做完。我們來試試看好嗎？」婷半信半疑。舊玻璃和紙筒真的能讓她看到什麼嗎？
那個週末他們就開始動手。婷急著開工，很快瀏覽了一下說明書，爺爺卻一行一行慢慢讀，還把每片鏡片舉到光線下仔細檢查。他指了指架子上的螺絲起子，婷便把固定鏡片的小螺絲鎖緊。第一個挫折很快就來了：他們把紙筒對準月亮，看到的卻一片模糊。爺爺解釋，兩片鏡片之間的距離不對，所以每天傍晚，他們都把鏡片挪動一點點，再測試一次。
一個星期後，婷開始失去耐心。「我們為什麼不直接上網買一台望遠鏡就好？」她問。爺爺笑了笑：「是可以啊。但買來的望遠鏡會把它運作的原理藏起來。我就喜歡兩片鏡片加一根紙筒的這種單純。我們找到的每個缺點，都在教我們一些東西。」接著他承認，小時候只因第一次失敗就放棄，實在是目光短淺。
十月的一個晴朗夜晚，他們把望遠鏡架在爺爺臥室的窗前。爺爺穿著拖鞋慢慢拖著步子走進來，婷推開那扇老舊的木製百葉窗。她把紙筒對準月亮，再調整一次，然後開心地尖叫起來。月球上的坑洞清晰銳利，就像有人把照片放大了一樣。爺爺在她身旁顯得平靜安詳，彷彿四十年前的心願終於悄悄實現了。
後來婷明白，他們做出來的不只是一架望遠鏡。把一個大問題簡化成許多小步驟的過程中，他們也培養出了耐心。

questions.stem: Why was Ting skeptical at first?
options: She doubted that old glass and a paper tube could show her anything.
She thought Grandpa had lost the instructions.
She had already bought a telescope online.
She did not like looking at the moon.
questions.explain: 第一段最後婷心想：舊玻璃和紙筒真的能讓她看到什麼嗎？可見她懷疑這些老東西做不出能用的望遠鏡，故選 (A)。(C) 她只是提議上網買，並沒有真的買。
questions.evidence: Could old glass and a paper tube really show her anything?

questions.stem: What caused their first setback?
options: The lenses were the wrong distance apart.
A page of the instructions was missing.
questions.explain: 第二段說他們看到的月亮一片模糊，爺爺解釋是兩片鏡片之間的距離不對，故選 (C)。其他選項文中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: The lenses, Grandpa explained, were the wrong distance apart

questions.stem: Why did Grandpa prefer not to buy a telescope?
options: He thought store-bought telescopes were too expensive.
He wanted them to understand how a telescope works and learn from its problems.
He did not know how to shop online.
He wanted to sell the one they built.
questions.explain: 爺爺說買來的望遠鏡會把運作原理藏起來，又說找到的每個缺點都在教他們東西，可見他重視親手了解原理、從問題中學習，故選 (B)。(A) 文中沒有提到價錢。
questions.evidence: But a store-bought one would hide how it works.

questions.stem: The word "serene" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 爺爺看著四十年的心願「悄悄實現」，神情 serene，可知是「平靜安詳的」，故選 (D)。(C) 吵鬧與「悄悄」的氣氛不符。
questions.evidence: Grandpa looked serene, as though a forty-year-old wish had quietly come true

vocab.stem: Many doctors were ______ about the new treatment at first, but years of careful testing proved that it worked.
vocab.explain: but 後面說多年測試證明有效，可知醫生們起初是「懷疑的」，故選 skeptical。serene（安詳的）、shabby（破舊的）、simultaneous（同時的）都無法和後面的轉折呼應。

vocab.stem: Short of time before the quiz, Amy could only ______ her notes, reading quickly to catch the main points instead of every word.
vocab.explain: 只讀重點、不讀每個字，就是「略讀、瀏覽」，故選 skim。shred（撕碎）、shriek（尖叫）、shuffle（洗牌；拖著腳走）都不符合快速閱讀的意思。

title: Born to Help?
paragraphs: Imagine you drop your pen in class. Before you can reach for it, a classmate picks it up and gives it back. Why do people help others when they gain nothing in return? For a long time, many thinkers believed that humans are selfish by nature and that kindness is just a [[sly|L6-0824]] way to win favors. Research in psychology and [[sociology|L6-0834]] now tells a more hopeful story.

In a well-known study published in 2006, researchers in Germany watched toddlers about eighteen months old. When an adult "accidentally" dropped an object and reached for it without success, many of the children walked over and picked it up for him without being asked or praised. Such [[spontaneous|L6-0849]] help suggests that the wish to assist others appears very early, before children have learned many social rules. Helping may be partly [[instinctive|L6-0457]].

Kindness also seems to benefit the helper. In a 2008 study in Canada, people were given a small amount of money and told to spend it either on themselves or on someone else. By the end of the day, those who had spent it on others reported feeling happier. Many volunteers describe a similar warm glow after helping, and some say that a small act of kindness lifted them out of a [[slump|L6-0823]].

Kindness also builds [[solidarity|L6-0836]]. After a storm or an earthquake, neighbors who rarely [[socialize|L6-0833]] often work side by side to clear streets and share food. On the sports field, [[sportsmanship|L6-0851]] earns respect, whether it means lending a pair of [[sneakers|L6-0826]] to a friend who forgot hers or stopping to check on a fallen rival. Even a few kind words to a [[sorrowful|L6-0840]] friend can [[enrich|L6-0307]] both lives.

None of this means that people are always kind. But the research suggests that kindness is not a [[sneaky|L6-0827]] trick. It is part of who we are, and like a muscle, it grows stronger with use. So the next time you see a classmate eating lunch in [[solitude|L6-0838]], you might simply sit down nearby and say hello. Small acts like this can grow into a [[lifelong|L6-0506]] habit.
zh: 想像你在課堂上掉了筆。你還來不及伸手，就有同學把它撿起來還給你。為什麼人會在得不到任何回報的情況下幫助別人？很長一段時間，許多思想家相信人類天生自私，善意只不過是一種討人情的狡猾手段。然而，心理學和社會學的研究現在說出了一個更令人樂觀的故事。
在 2006 年發表的一項知名研究中，德國的研究人員觀察大約十八個月大的幼兒。當一位大人「不小心」掉了東西、伸手卻搆不到時，許多孩子會走過去幫他撿起來，而且沒有人要求、也沒有人誇獎他們。這種自發的幫助顯示，想幫助別人的念頭很早就出現了，甚至在孩子學會許多社會規範之前。幫助別人，可能有一部分是出於本能。
善意似乎也對幫助者本身有好處。在 2008 年加拿大的一項研究中，受試者拿到一小筆錢，並被告知要花在自己身上或別人身上。到了當天結束時，把錢花在別人身上的人表示自己比較快樂。許多志工也描述過幫助別人後那種暖暖的感覺，有些人說，一個小小的善行曾帶他們走出低潮。
善意也能建立團結。在暴風雨或地震過後，平時很少往來的鄰居常常並肩清理街道、分享食物。在運動場上，運動家精神會贏得尊重，不論是把一雙運動鞋借給忘了帶的朋友，或是停下來關心跌倒的對手。即使只是對一位悲傷的朋友說幾句溫暖的話，也能讓雙方的生命更加豐富。
這並不表示人永遠都很善良。但研究顯示，善意並不是什麼偷偷摸摸的伎倆，而是我們本性的一部分；它就像肌肉一樣，越用越強壯。所以下次你看到同學獨自一人吃午餐時，也許可以在旁邊坐下來打聲招呼。像這樣的小舉動，可能會成為一輩子的習慣。

questions.stem: What did many of the toddlers in the 2006 study do?
options: They refused to share their toys with the adult.
They picked up an object the adult dropped, without being asked.
They copied everything the adult did.
They asked the adult for a reward.

title: The Library That Wanted Every Book
paragraphs: Over two thousand years ago, the kings of Egypt set out on a bold project in the port city of Alexandria: to collect every book in the known world. Their library became the most famous of ancient times. Its shelves did not hold books with pages but [[scrolls|L6-0790]], long rolls of papyrus, a paper-like material made from a plant that grew along the Nile.

The kings pursued their goal with [[relentless|L6-0748]] energy. According to one ancient story, every ship that entered the harbor was searched for books. Any books found were copied by hand; the library kept the originals and gave the owners the copies. Egypt's [[royalty|L6-0778]] also competed with other kingdoms. A [[rivalry|L6-0773]] with the city of Pergamum was said to be so fierce that Egypt stopped selling papyrus to it, so Pergamum began writing on animal skins instead. Historians [[reckon|L6-0731]] this tale is more legend than fact, but it shows how [[priceless|L6-0696]] books were.

Scholars came from across the Mediterranean to study there. To help readers [[retrieve|L6-0765]] the right scroll from tens of thousands, the poet Callimachus [[compiled|L6-0168]] a huge list of authors and their works, an early guide to the collection. The scrolls included poetry, [[prose|L6-0703]], mathematics, and medicine, and careful [[scrutiny|L6-0791]] of them led to great achievements. Eratosthenes, who once directed the library, used shadows in two cities to estimate the size of the Earth with surprising accuracy.

How did the library disappear? Although many people imagine a single great fire, most historians believe its decline was slow. Fire was one [[setback|L6-0801]]; the bigger problem was a lack of money and support over the centuries. Papyrus breaks down in damp air, so scrolls had to be copied again and again. When support ended, no one was left to [[salvage|L6-0783]] the aging collection. No scroll from the library is known to survive today.

Yet the dream has not died. In 2002, a new library opened near the old site, a [[revival|L6-0767]] of the ancient spirit. Its round, sloping roof is [[reminiscent|L6-0753]] of the sun rising from the sea. The Internet, which lets anyone [[skim|L6-0816]] millions of pages in seconds, is a modern form of the kings' dream. The lesson of Alexandria is a [[solemn|L6-0835]] one: knowledge survives only when people keep caring for it.
zh: 兩千多年前，埃及的國王們在港口城市亞歷山卓展開一項大膽的計畫：收集已知世界裡的每一本書。他們的圖書館成為古代最有名的圖書館。館中書架上放的不是有頁面的書，而是卷軸——用莎草紙做成的長卷，莎草紙是一種類似紙的材料，由尼羅河沿岸生長的植物製成。
國王們以毫不鬆懈的熱情追求這個目標。根據一則古老的故事，每艘進港的船都會被搜查是否帶著書。找到的書會被人用手抄寫一份；圖書館留下原本，把抄本交給書的主人。埃及王室也和其他王國互相競爭。據說他們和帕加馬城的競爭非常激烈，埃及甚至停止賣莎草紙給對方，於是帕加馬改在獸皮上書寫。歷史學家認為這個故事比較像傳說而不是事實，但它顯示出書在當時有多麼珍貴。
學者們從地中海各地來到這裡研究。為了幫助讀者從數萬卷書中找到需要的卷軸，詩人卡利馬科斯編了一份龐大的作者與作品清單，可說是館藏指南的早期版本。館藏包括詩歌、散文、數學和醫學，學者對這些作品的仔細鑽研帶來了偉大的成就。曾經主持圖書館的埃拉托斯特尼，利用兩座城市的影子，以驚人的準確度估算出地球的大小。
這座圖書館是怎麼消失的？雖然很多人想像是一場大火，但大多數歷史學家認為它是慢慢衰落的。火災只是其中一次挫折；更大的問題是數百年來資金與支持的不足。莎草紙在潮濕的空氣中會損壞，所以卷軸必須一再重新抄寫。當支持中斷後，就再也沒有人能搶救這些日漸老舊的藏書。如今已知沒有任何一卷來自這座圖書館的卷軸留存下來。
然而，這個夢想並沒有消失。2002 年，一座新的圖書館在舊址附近開幕，是古代精神的復興。它圓形而傾斜的屋頂讓人聯想到從海上升起的太陽。網路讓任何人都能在幾秒內瀏覽數百萬頁的資料，也是國王們夢想的現代版本。亞歷山卓給我們的教訓十分沉重：知識只有在人們持續珍惜照顧時才能留存。
